November 12, 2026




 Spain beat Czech Republic to retain perfect Nations League record 







PRAGUE, Czech Republic (AFP)—Alex Baena scored from the spot, and Marc Pubill added another in the second half as Spain beat a ten-man Czech Republic 2-0 in the Nations League in Prague on Thursday.

The win leaves Spain unbeaten in 44 competitive games in a row, including five wins in as many Nations League games this season.

Spain, who already secured a quarter-final berth before travelling to Prague, will face England in Madrid on Sunday in their final Group A3 game.

Baena scored in the 39th minute after a VAR check revealed Czech midfielder Lukas Ambros had handled the ball inside the box.

The Atletico Madrid winger blasted his spot kick past Matej Kovar, who touched the ball but failed to clear it.

Czech captain Ladislav Krejci was sent off in the 69th minute after bringing down second-half substitute Roberto Fernandez on a counter-attack.

It was a deja-vu for the Wolverhampton defender, who also got a red card at the end of Spain’s 3-1 home win over the Czechs last month.

Pubill, another substitute, beat Eindhoven goalkeeper Kovar with a clinical low shot deep into stoppage time after robbing Tomas Soucek.

“I want to appreciate the work of the entire team,” said Spain coach Luis de la Fuente.

“It was a difficult game against an energetic team with an aggressive style. We had moments when it cost us a lot of energy to control the game.”

De la Fuentes missed Lamine Yamal, Dani Olmo, Rodri and Eric Garcia with injuries while Mikel Oyarzabal was sidelined with flu.

Spain got off to a slow start on the chilly evening but never really let the hosts get close throughout the first half.

They gradually stepped up their pressure, often confining the Czechs to their box and looking for chances.

– Yamal, Oyarzabal to return –

Fabian Ruiz hit the post with a curling right-footer three minutes from halftime, while Dean Huijsen’s header found Kovar’s arms.

Yeremy Pino, replacing Yamal on the right flank, saw his goal overturned by VAR for offside just two minutes into the second half.

The Czechs showed higher spirits after the break, but David Zima tipped the ball over the bar from close range and Adam Hlozek’s glancing header landed on the top of the crossbar.

The Czechs lost momentum after the red card, but Baena had two efforts cleared by Kovar and Fernandez saw his shot stopped by Kovar and then hit the post.

“The score could have been higher but we struggled with the finish,” said de la Fuente.

He added Yamal and Oyarzabal would rejoin the team ahead of the England game.

“We have good news, they will join us tomorrow and will be ready for the England game,” he continued. “If everything goes well, they can both play 90 minutes.”

The hosts, led by de la Fuente’s long-time collaborator Santi Denia, have lost all their Nations League games this season.

They are next travelling to Croatia for a game they need to win to stay in the top tier of the competition for the next edition.

 Jamaican man wanted by police nabbed in Trinidad 







PORT OF SPAIN, Trinidad (CMC) – A 60-year-old Jamaican man wanted in connection with several serious offences in Jamaica has been arrested in Trinidad and Tobago following the issuance of an Interpol Red Notice.

The Trinidad and Tobago Police Service (TTPS) said in a statement on Wednesday that officers from the Criminal Investigation Department, Criminal Records Office, Immigration Investigations Unit and Anti-Kidnapping Unit conducted an operation between 9:00 am and 3:00 pm on Tuesday.

During the operation, officers went to a location on Cumuto Road, Barrackpore, where they arrested Dockery Courtney Radcliffe, who was the subject of the Red Notice.

Radcliffe is wanted in Jamaica on charges of robbery with aggravation, rape, grievous sexual assault and abduction.

He remains in police custody and is expected to be processed by the Immigration Enforcement Unit as extradition proceedings are pursued.

An Interpol Red Notice is a request to law enforcement agencies worldwide to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition, surrender or similar legal action.

 From Deed to Key heads to Manhattan for investment and housing conference 







Manhattan is gearing up to welcome a dynamic contingent of real estate developers, realtors, attorneys, financial experts, commissioned land surveyors and sustainable development specialists for the From Deed to Key Investment & Housing Conference & Marketplace — New York Edition, taking place on Saturday, November 14, 2026, at The Westin New York Grand Central, 212 East 42nd Street.

Following its inaugural staging in South Florida in June 2026, From Deed to Key is doing it again — this time in the heart of Manhattan, bringing together industry leaders, investors, entrepreneurs and members of the Caribbean diaspora under the theme “Invest in Your Piece of Di Rock.”

The conference aims to bridge the gap between investment aspirations and action, connecting attendees with the professional expertise, financial guidance and opportunities needed to navigate property ownership, real estate development and wealth creation in Jamaica.

The conference will feature an impressive lineup of industry professionals, including Michelle Thomas, attorney-at-law, of Michelle Thomas & Associates, who will address the legal complexities of buying, selling and protecting property investments.

Mark Nelson of So Cal Credit Repairs will share critical insights into credit readiness and mortgage preparedness, while Al Junior Taylor, commissioned land surveyor, will highlight the importance of land surveys, property boundaries and due diligence before purchasing or developing land.

Adding further depth to the discussions are Jhanine Jackson, sales manager, VM Property Services Ltd, who will share insights into real estate opportunities, property acquisition and investment, and Richard May, sustainable development advisor and CEO of PowerSource Jamaica, who will explore sustainable development, resilient construction and innovative approaches to building for the future.

Together, these professionals will equip attendees with practical knowledge spanning legal ownership, financing, land surveying, real estate acquisition, sustainable development and long-term wealth creation.

Adding diplomatic significance to the occasion, the event is proudly endorsed by Jamaica’s Consul General to New York, Oliver Mair, who will deliver official greetings and share insights on diaspora engagement, investment opportunities and strengthening economic ties with Jamaica.

For Maxine Miller, founder of From Deed to Key and Managing Director of Black Ink Marketing & Event Solutions, the New York staging represents another significant step in building a platform that connects the diaspora with credible professionals and meaningful investment opportunities.

“We are doing it again, and this time we are bringing From Deed to Key to the heart of Manhattan! We have assembled an extraordinary contingent of professionals who are not simply coming to speak, but to share knowledge, open doors, and help people make informed investment decisions.

“Too many people in the diaspora want to own property, build a home or invest in Jamaica, but are uncertain about where to begin or whom to trust. From Deed to Key was created to bridge that gap. This is about moving beyond conversations into action — creating ownership, opportunity and generational wealth,” Miller stated.

Miller also welcomed the consul general’s endorsement, describing it as an important affirmation of the initiative’s mission to strengthen connections between Jamaica and its overseas communities.

A major highlight of the event is the From Deed to Key Marketplace, an interactive space bringing together real estate developers, realtors, financial institutions, legal professionals and other industry experts, providing attendees with direct access to property investment opportunities and professional guidance.

Featured developers Milford Ridge Homes and Richmond will showcase residential developments and investment opportunities in Jamaica, offering prospective buyers and investors an opportunity to engage directly with developers and explore their options for property ownership.

Realtors will also be on hand to guide attendees through available properties, purchasing processes and investment considerations, while financial and legal professionals will provide valuable insights into financing, due diligence and protecting property investments.

The Marketplace is designed to move beyond conversations, creating an environment where attendees can ask questions, explore opportunities, establish meaningful business connections and take practical steps towards turning their property ownership ambitions into reality.

The conference will culminate in a Cocktail Networking Mixer from 6:00 pm to 8:00 pm, bringing together speakers, sponsors, exhibitors and delegates for an evening of networking and relationship-building.

The event is supported by VM Group and So Cal Credit Repairs, with Richie B Radio serving as the official media partner, alongside other participating organisations.

With New York home to a vibrant Jamaican and Caribbean diaspora, the conference presents a timely opportunity for individuals seeking to purchase property, regularise land ownership, develop existing assets or explore investment opportunities in Jamaica.

“You may have the dream, you may have the land, you may even have the deed — but what comes next? That is the conversation we are bringing to Manhattan. We want people to leave empowered, informed and ready to take action,” Miller added.

news.title: Russia-China-US meeting should take mutual concerns into account — Chinese newspaper
news.text:
BEIJING, November 13. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin’s possible trilateral meeting with his counterparts from China and the United States, Xi Jinping and Donald Trump, should take concerns of all parties into account, Chinese analysts told the Global Times newspaper.

In an article about the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, where the meeting may take place, Chinese experts say the sides should address each other’s concerns on equal terms.

Global Times said international media closely follow news about the potential meeting. For example, from November 1 to 12, the Chinese foreign ministry fielded questions from journalists on the subject five times, confirming each time that Beijing is maintaining contacts with Moscow and Washington on the matter.

Zhang Jiadong, a professor at the Center for American Studies, Fudan University, told the newspaper that Washington’s determination to hold the meeting "partly stems from its desire to notch up diplomatic wins on the global stage and project its diplomatic clout." In the expert’s opinion, an event in this format "would carry substantial political symbolism, especially amid the current international landscape and the backdrop of US domestic politics."

Meanwhile, Yang Xiyu, a senior research fellow at the China Institute of International Studies, believes that the US may also hope that "the potential gathering can reinstate relevant dialogue mechanisms and put guardrails around risks tied to US-Russia relations and the Ukraine conflict, preventing the situation from spiraling out of control."

The 33rd APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting will be held in Shenzhen from November 18 to 19 under the theme "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together." The Russian delegation to the event in south China’s Shenzhen will be led by President Vladimir Putin. According to Russian Foreign Ministry Ambassador-at-Large Marat Berdyev, this demonstrates the importance Russia attaches to developing economic ties with its partners in the Asia-Pacific region, particularly China.

news.title: Dan Sullivan Timeline: How Trump’s Posts Tracked DOJ’s Alaska Senate Fight
news.text: A week after Alaska's polls closed, with ballots still being counted, President Donald Trump returned to the race he could not stop writing about. "Dan Sullivan PLUS Dan Sullivan," he posted on Truth Social Tuesday. He demanded that every vote for a retired Petersburg schoolteacher be handed to the Republican senator who shares his name, and called the contest a "rigged election." Alaska’s ballot does not work that way. Votes move only through rankings voters made themselves, and only if no candidate wins more than 50 percent of first-choice votes. In that case, the state runs a ranked-choice tabulation on November 18. But the post was the latest entry in a record that runs back to April. Newsweek logged more than 30 dated events: presidential posts, court filings, Justice Department statements and actions by Alaska officials. The record does not show that the posts caused the department's moves. The federal inquiry began before the heaviest posting. It shows something narrower. Twice this fall, a presidential post was followed within a day by a Justice Department legal action—and twice more, his words and the department’s landed on the same news day. And when asked who wanted the government's lawsuit, the president and his attorney general gave different answers. A Count Still Open As of 10:59 p.m. Eastern November 12, the Alaska Division of Elections unofficial results showed Democrat Mary Peltola with 125,157 first-choice votes and Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan with 119,357. Republican Gerald L. Heikes had 5,490, and Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. had 4,199. As of 11:01 p.m. Eastern, the Associated Press estimated 88 percent of the vote counted and had not called the race. Absentee ballots mailed within the U.S. and postmarked by Election Day are accepted through November 13, and overseas ballots can arrive through November 18. Certification is targeted for November 25. A Name on a Ballot The record begins with the voting system itself. On April 10, Trump called Alaska's ranked-choice voting "disastrous, and very fraudulent." Around May 29, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., a retired fifth-grade teacher from the fishing town of Petersburg, filed to run for the Senate, according to the Justice Department's complaint. The state's elections director tried to remove him from the ballot, and Alaska's courts restored him in late June. On July 3, ABC News reported that the department had opened an investigation into his campaign. That came before almost every presidential post on the subject. On primary day, August 18, Trump wrote: "VOTE FOR THE REAL DAN SULLIVAN TODAY." That same day, Reuters reported that the department had issued grand jury subpoenas, citing a source familiar with the probe. Three Days in October The pattern is clearest in late October. At 10:28 p.m. Eastern on October 21, Trump wrote on Truth Social that the administration was weighing "powerful legal options to remove the fraudulent Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. from the Ballot." On Thursday, before anything was filed, Attorney General Todd Blanche, Trump's former personal lawyer, told reporters it is "never our intention" to improperly interfere with certification. Later that day, the department sued Alaska. The complaint asked a judge to block certification of any result that votes for Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. could have changed. It was signed by Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward, who had represented Trump allies and January 6 defendants. On Friday, Trump landed in Florida and settled the question of where the suit came from. "I'm the one that said do it," he told reporters. Two Accounts of One Lawsuit On Saturday, Blanche wrote on X that the suit "was written by Justice Department attorneys" and relied solely on federal law. He did not say who had asked for it. Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski, who had endorsed Sullivan, said the department "should never have filed this lawsuit." At 11:13 p.m. Eastern, Trump called Alaska's ballot "a TOTAL DEMOCRAT SCAM meant to confuse the Voter." The next day, Peltola's lawyers quoted that post in a court filing. On Sunday, Blanche told CNN that Trump was not trying to overturn Alaska's results "in any way, shape or form." On CBS' Face the Nation, Margaret Brennan asked who Trump had told to file the suit. "I will never, ever, ever talk about communications that I have with the president of the United States," Blanche said. Asked whom Trump meant by "I'm the one that said do it," he said he had no idea, and would not say if he did. The president says he gave the order. His attorney general says he does not know to whom. The two accounts have never been squared. The Week Everything Moved On October 28, The New York Times reported that people tied to Peltola's campaign and aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee had helped push the Petersburg candidate onto the ballot. The report relied partly on a fired former campaign manager who later tried to retract her comments. The campaign and the DSCC denied involvement. That day, Trump wrote that Peltola "should suffer the Legal and Political consequences." Blanche told Fox News to expect more from the department "this week." Governor Mike Dunleavy ordered a state investigation. Within a day, the department had issued a new round of grand jury subpoenas, and filed an amended complaint that drew on the press reports. On November 1, U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason dismissed the suit for lack of standing. Setting ballots aside for investigators, she found, was not something the court "can or should order." Within two hours, the government said it would appeal. Early on Election Day, Trump posted that the Petersburg candidate was "MISSING IN ACTION." That day, news broke that prosecutors had sent target letters to Democratic attorney Marc Elias and others. After the Polls Closed The posts outlasted the voting. On November 5, Trump wrote that the votes for the "Fake Dan Sullivan" belonged to the senator: "There is no other fair solution!" On November 8, Dunleavy told a radio host that state investigators were examining "anything that might resemble perjury." The appeal is moving more slowly. The department's opening brief is not due until December 14, weeks after Alaska plans to certify. Unless a candidate wins more than 50 percent of first-choice votes, the state will run its ranked-choice tabulation on November 18 and show where Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.'s voters placed their second choices. It will show where those ballots went, not why. The state's own lawyers told the court that no pattern of ballot markings will reveal a voter's reason for choosing him. The teacher from Petersburg has said almost nothing since summer. In August, he told The New York Times he hoped voters could tell an incumbent senator from a teacher. news.title: SpaceX and Tesla talks on record merger are said to progress
news.text:
SpaceX and Tesla Inc. are progressing in their merger negotiations, setting the stage for a combination that could redefine the limits of global dealmaking.

Elon Musk’s two largest companies could announce what would be the biggest-ever deal as soon as in December, according to people familiar with the matter. That aggressive timeline reflects Musk’s tendency to move quickly when it comes to corporate maneuvers.

The companies have also discussed a scenario in which an announcement slips into early 2027, said the people, who asked to not be identified because the discussions are private. Their boards and advisers are hammering out the terms of the tie-up and governance structure of the combined entity, among other matters, the people said.

Representatives for Tesla and SpaceX didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

Tesla shares jumped to a session high, rising as much as 1.9%, while SpaceX stock gained 0.5% as of 3:20 p.m. Thursday in New York.

The merger would be a blockbuster for Wall Street’s dealmakers, creating a conglomerate housing electric vehicles, energy storage batteries, rockets and satellites. The rationale for bringing all those assets under one roof lies in a shared ambition to leverage artificial intelligence across space, driverless cars and humanoid robots.

But both companies will have to grapple with obstacles before they can close a transaction, including how to ring-fence Tesla’s operations in China, according to the people.

National security sensitivities around SpaceX’s US government and defense contracts, and Tesla’s large, profitable China manufacturing footprint, loom as “key dynamics that are at odds with each other” when it comes to getting regulatory and shareholder approvals for a deal, JPMorgan analyst Rajat Gupta told clients in a research note last month.

The merger would be a major test case for political sentiment following the US midterm elections. Democrats, which took control of Congress, have pledged to probe Musk’s business and political dealings.

Musk in October said the boards of the companies had formed special committees of independent board directors to consider combining.

SpaceX has a market value of more than $1.9 trillion following its initial public offering, while Tesla is worth about $1.5 trillion. Tesla is slated to host its annual shareholder meeting on Dec. 3.

Bloomberg News had reported that SpaceX and Tesla were pushing to announce a deal by the first half of next year, with the aim of closing the merger before the end of President Donald Trump’s term. One of the factors being discussed is the number of shares SpaceX will have to offer Tesla investors in the transaction.

SpaceX and Tesla already have business ties, including a joint effort to build a semiconductor plant in Texas called Terafab. The companies also increasingly have been laying the groundwork for joint operations.

SpaceX, formally known as Space Exploration Technologies Corp. and based in Starbase, Texas, went public in June in a landmark listing in New York that made Musk the world’s first trillionaire.

The company has transformed in recent years from a leading rocket manufacturer and launch provider into a crucial supplier of AI infrastructure to companies including Anthropic PBC as well as a top provider of internet beamed down from space.

news.title: Trump Says He'd Beat Obama 'Easily' in Potential Presidential Race
news.text: President Donald Trump said that he could "easily" beat former President Barack Obama in a hypothetical matchup, while calling his predecessor "highly overrated." In a sit-down with Stephen A. Smith on Smith's podcast Straight Shooter on Thursday, Trump said, "I got many more votes than he got. And I got many more votes in the states...I have most of the state records of the big states. If you take a look at Texas, I have the all-time record, Florida I have the all-time record." Smith then asked Trump if he was implying that he'd beat Obama, "Yeah, I think I'd beat him easily, yeah. I think he's highly overrated." In the 2024 presidential election, Trump won all the swing states and the popular vote with 77,304,290 votes compared to Vice President Kamala Harris' 75,019,761 votes. In the 2012 election, Obama defeated Republican Mitt Romney with 62,611,250 votes compared to 59,134,475 votes. Trump's remarks to Smith come on the heels of sweeping midterm losses for the Republican Party that saw House and Senate majority flip in favor of the Democrats. The president conceded partially that the landslide Democratic wins could be due to the war in Iran, although he said he would still do it again. Similarly, Democrats lost the midterms in 2010 while Obama was in office. Newsweek reached out to the office of Barack and Michelle Obama via online portal Thursday night for comment. What To Know In his comments to Smith about Obama, Trump added, "I just think, that's just my opinion, I think he's overrated. I didn't think he was a good president, I thought he was a divider." Smith then asked Trump how he'd classify himself, which he answered, "as a person that brings people together." In the 2024 presidential election cycle, Trump obtained 6,110,125 votes in Florida versus 4,683,038 votes for Harris, according to the Florida Department of State Division of Elections. In 2012, Obama obtained 4,237,756 votes in the Sunshine State and Romney landed 4,163,447 votes. In state voting data reviewed by Newsweek dating over 40 years, Trump had the most votes for a presidential nominee in Florida. In Texas, Trump obtained 6,393,597 votes compared to Harris' 4,835,250 votes in the 2024 presidential election. In 2012, Obama had 3,294,440 votes in the Lone Star State compared to Romney's 4,555,799 votes. Newsweek also reviewed state voting data going back decades in Texas, and Trump had the most votes out of any presidential nominee. Texas has been known as a Republican stronghold for presidential elections, and Florida has shifted to the right over time and is now also seen as a reliable pickup for GOP presidential candidates. Robert Collins, professor of public policy at Dillard University, told Newsweek on Thursday: "This is clearly just President Trump throwing red meat to his base. Given the president currently has a national job approval rating in the 30s, no rational observer believes he could beat Obama in a head-to-head matchup right now. "His past remarks on the possibility of running for a third term are also just trying to keep his base happy. No serious constitutional scholar believes there is any legal way for President Trump to run for a third term." The president's interview with Smith also touched on Iran, working with Democrats during the remainder of his term, gasoline prices, immigration policy and his legacy. Trump and Obama's Popularity & Approval Compared In a CNN-SSRS poll conducted earlier this year, 57 percent said they had a favorable opinion of Obama versus 32 percent who had an unfavorable opinion. Comparatively, Trump had a 34 percent favorability rating versus a 55 percent unfavorable rating. When asked which president they admire the most, Obama landed 30 percent and Trump had 19 percent, the poll shows. The poll was conducted from May 7 to May 31 among 2,480 respondents and had a margin of error of 2.7 percent. In a YouGov/Economist poll this week, Trump's approval rating is 32 percent versus a 63 percent disapproval rating. The poll surveyed 1,685 U.S. citizens from November 9 to November 11 and had a margin of error of 3 percent. In a November 2010 poll after the midterm elections, Obama's approval was 42 percent with a 49 percent disapproval rating, also in a YouGov/Economist poll.  Guyana grants eighth offshore oil development 







GEORGETOWN, Guyana (CMC)—The Guyana government has approved its eighth offshore petroleum development, granting a production licence for the Longtail Project, which will become the country’s first non-associated gas (NAG) development.

The Ministry of Natural Resources said the approval covers the Longtail Field Development Plan (FDP) and the issuance of the corresponding Petroleum Production Licence (PPL), marking a step towards the development and commercialisation of Guyana’s natural gas resources.

The project will be operated by ExxonMobil Guyana Limited, alongside co-venturers Hess Guyana Exploration Limited and CNOOC Petroleum Guyana Limited, and will target nine reservoirs in the Stabroek Block.

According to the ministry, the development will use a newly built Floating Production, Storage and Offloading (FPSO) vessel with the capacity to handle approximately 1.2 billion cubic feet of gas per day and produce up to 250,000 barrels of condensate daily.

The project is expected to produce approximately 776 million barrels of condensate over a 30-year period, using 27 production wells and 18 gas injection wells. First production is anticipated before the end of 2030.

The development will include facilities for full gas reinjection and eventual gas exports to support onshore utilisation.

The ministry said the Longtail production licence includes requirements for a gas utilisation and export study, covering reservoir performance, production forecasts, export timelines and potential gas markets.

It also includes provisions for gas export safety and risk management systems, as well as requirements for the FPSOs’ base design to incorporate the necessary gas export facilities.

The project is also expected to support President Irfaan Ali’s plans for a natural gas industrial site in Berbice, including a second offshore Gas-to-Energy pipeline.

The proposed industrial development is intended to provide gas for electricity generation and support new industries, including fertiliser production, alumina and mineral processing, data centres and other energy-intensive activities.

The government has said the initiative is expected to attract investment, create employment and expand economic activity beyond the petroleum sector.

The Longtail Project adds to Guyana’s growing offshore petroleum portfolio, while opening another avenue for the development of its natural gas resources.

news.title: Air Force One To Spy Scandal: A Timeline Of Trump And Jensen Huang's Ties
news.text: President Donald Trump's close ties with billionaire Jensen Huang have come under renewed scrutiny after revelations about the former Nvidia CEO's affairs, including with a businesswoman alleged to be a spy for China.Trump has said he was "amazed" after the revelations concerning one of his closest allies in Silicon Valley. Huang resigned on November 12 and faces an FBI probe and congressional hearings.Over the past two years, Huang has voiced support for the Trump administration's AI agenda and met the Republican leader many times as Nvidia sought to sell advanced chips to the Chinese market and lobbied for looser restrictions on Chinese access to Nvidia's sophisticated AI chips. Democratic and Republican lawmakers have called to halt exports of advanced AI chips to China. Huang and the White House have argued that continuing US sales to China would keep Chinese customers reliant on US technology. Here is a timeline on some publicly known interactions and meetings between Huang and Trump since the Republican leader returned to the White House in January 2025:JANUARY 2025:Trump met Huang during the first month of his return to the White House, casting the interaction as a good meeting. JULY 2025:The then-Nvidia CEO met Trump at the White House before Huang's visit to China. Later in the month, Trump gave a shout out to Huang as he spoke and signed executive orders at an AI summit. "Jensen, will you stand up? What a job, what a job you've done," Trump remarked. "He's a great guy too."AUGUST 2025:Huang met Trump at the White House as the Trump administration and Nvidia engaged in talks over allowing advanced AI chip sales to China.SEPTEMBER 2025:Huang joined Trump during a state visit to Britain.NOVEMBER 2025:Huang attended a US-Saudi Arabia investment forum in Washington during the first visit of Saudi Arabian Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to the US capital since 2018. Huang talked about the future of AI at the event.DECEMBER 2025:Trump praised Huang when the then-Nvidia CEO visited Washington and met the Republican leader, who said the chip executive was aware of where he stood on export controls.Huang was in the US capital that day to meet lawmakers and told them that state-by-state US regulations would slow the progress of AI development.JANUARY 2026:The Trump administration began allowing some exports of Nvidia's powerful H200 AI chips to China on a case-by-case basis but it did not lift the restrictions applying to organizations that Washington had put on a trade restriction list.MARCH 2026:In late March, the White House announced Huang as part of a 13-member council formally called the "President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology" to weigh in on AI policy and other issues.MAY 2026:Huang was among a delegation of tech CEOs who joined Trump during his visit to China to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping as the Republican leader aimed to urge Beijing to "open up" to US business. Trump, in a last minute addition to his May trip to China, asked Huang to join him. Huang was spotted boarding Air Force One during a re-fuelling stop in Alaska en route to Beijing.SEPTEMBER 2026:As the Trump administration and AI companies faced increasing scrutiny over risks posed by advanced AI, Trump said on September 29 that Huang was among a number of AI CEOs who signed a voluntary safety pact and backed data center expansion. Huang met Trump at the White House that day along with a number of tech executives. Trump, who had argued previously that the US does not need new AI-specific regulations, said the pact was "morally binding," prompting criticism that it did not lay out consequences for non-compliance.In the previous week, Huang attended a high-profile state dinner for Xi at the White House when the Chinese leader met Trump.In mid-September, Huang addressed AI safety concerns during a summit in Los Angeles. He took a phone call from Trump during the event and put him on speaker for the audience. During the roughly five-minute call, Trump called AI safety fears a "hoax." OCTOBER 2026:In early October, Trump awarded the National Medal of Science, the United States' highest honor for scientists and engineers, to Huang and some other tech industry leaders.The same day Trump gave him the award, the president disclosed buying up to $1.6 million and selling up to $1 million in Nvidia stock during the summer of 2026.The Washington Post reported in mid-October that Nvidia committed $25 million for Trump's planned White House ballroom.NOVEMBER 2026:Trump said on November 9 that he spoke to the then-Nvidia boss after the affair between Huang and Alice Huang - an unrelated former executive of Singapore-based company Megaspeed, whom US authorities suspected to be a Chinese spy - became public.Trump said the tech billionaire told him he had no idea that the woman was a spy and that Trump believed him."I asked him that question 'Did you have any idea that she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea that she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told a White House briefing."I know the FBI is looking into it," Trump said. "I think that he'll be in good shape."When asked about Huang's resignation on November 12, Trump said in a podcast interview that it was "sad" while describing him as a "tremendous talent.""I spoke to him yesterday (November 11), he is going through hell," Trump said in the podcast.The New York Times later reported Trump called him on November 10 and asked him to fight for his job.(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)

 Haitian forces recapture national stadium from gang control 







PORT-AU-PRINCE, Haiti—Haitian security forces regained control Thursday of the country’s main stadium that had been under gang control for two years, forcing the national football team to play elsewhere.

The Haitian National Police said in a statement that it had taken “full control” of the venue with the Task Force, a private security group serving the government, after which it left the stadium under the guard of Salvadoran soldiers.

The operation is part of the deployment of some 2,000 soldiers ordered by El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele, who announced last Tuesday that his men had destroyed the “headquarters” of 400 Mawozo, one of Haiti’s main gangs.

Bukele, who has gained attention for bringing Salvadoran gangs to heel but been accused of human rights violations, ordered the dispatch of the contingent to rescue four Salvadoran soldiers who went missing after an ambush on October 18 in Port-au-Prince.

The four soldiers are part of the Gang Suppression Force (GSF), a multinational group backed by the UN that distances itself from the actions of the troops sent for the rescue mission.

The Haitian police added that after retaking the Sylvio Cator Stadium, the Salvadoran military took charge of security there.

Salvadoran state-run television said Salvadoran forces “took up position” in the stadium on Thursday.

In 2024, the 10,000-capacity stadium fell into the hands of gangs that control much of the country, the poorest in Latin America and the Caribbean.

The violence forced the Haitian national football team to play World Cup qualifying matches in Curacao rather than at home.

The team, consisting virtually entirely of players who do not live in Haiti, won qualification to the World Cup in 2026 but were eliminated in the group stage.

news.title: Nvidia crisis prompts scrutiny of Lutnick’s role in chip policy
news.text:
Fallout from Jensen Huang’s ouster as Nvidia Corp. chief executive officer is reaching deep into Washington, where Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has drawn scrutiny over whether his department did enough to keep the company’s prized artificial intelligence chips out of China’s hands.

As the ultimate overseer of US export control programs, Lutnick would be accountable for any policy or enforcement gaps that allowed Nvidia’s AI processors to reach unauthorized Chinese buyers. For now, the Commerce chief has the blessing of President Donald Trump, who gave Lutnick a vote of confidence hours after Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation on Thursday.

Huang’s abrupt departure was prompted by revelations that he’d had an affair with a woman suspected by US officials of spying for China and whose Singapore-based company Megaspeed had been under investigation by Commerce for possible export control violations. Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing, while the former Nvidia chief’s romantic partner, Alice Huang, is now in China.

In the aftermath, Congress is demanding answers from Lutnick and other Trump administration officials about decisions that may have made it easier for China to obtain Nvidia’s advanced semiconductors as well as the degree to which Silicon Valley leaders like Jensen Huang may have influenced policy. 

Pressure on the administration and the tech sector is escalating a week after an election where voters expressed intense frustrations over the impact of the AI boom.

“I would like for Secretary Lutnick ASAP to come testify before the Senate Banking Committee because we have a lot of bipartisan questions and concerns about what’s happened over the last year,” Senator Jim Banks, an Indiana Republican, said in an interview on Fox News.

Axios reported on Wednesday that Trump had authorized a new crackdown on companies suspected of diverting advanced AI chips to China, but that Lutnick delayed acting on the directive. Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi, an Illinois Democrat, called the report “deeply, deeply disturbing.”

On at least three separate occasions earlier this year — in May, August and earlier this month — Trump approved taking action against suspected diversions of Nvidia chips to China, Axios reported.

This week’s events are “a freaking disaster at this point, and it deserves tremendous scrutiny not only by obviously Nvidia’s board, but by the intelligence community and the US government as well,” Krishnamoorthi said in an interview on Bloomberg Television Wednesday.

Further complicating the dynamic are allegations by Democratic lawmakers that Lutnick’s sons, who hold leadership positions at Cantor Fitzgerald, are profiting off of policy decisions that he makes. Lutnick, who previously was CEO of Cantor, divested his stake as legally required before becoming secretary, and elevated his sons to top jobs at the firm.

People with ties to the White House, who asked not to be identified describing private conversations, said Lutnick has been marginalized within the administration for a while. At the same time, his exit has been predicted before but it has not happened.

A White House official, who requested anonymity, said in an emailed statement that Trump maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position as the most transformative commerce secretary in modern history.

The Commerce Department didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Cantor Fitzgerald declined to comment.

One element of the Nvidia imbroglio is a little-known but powerful Commerce Department agency that’s known as the Bureau of Industry and Security and falls under Lutnick’s jurisdiction. 

BIS regulates exports of a wide range of products — including advanced AI chips — and it’s set to face renewed scrutiny as lawmakers threaten probes into the bureau’s leader, Under Secretary of Commerce Jeffrey Kessler.

The Senate Banking committee is already planning inquiries into Lutnick and Kessler’s decision-making. The two men “must explain why they have not closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China’s military,” Senator Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the committee, said in a statement.

In late summer 2025, Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter called Kessler to ask whether BIS was involved in the Singapore government’s recent detention of Alice Huang, Bloomberg News reported this week. BIS was not involved in that action, Bloomberg reported earlier, citing people familiar with the matter.

An Nvidia spokesperson has said that Teter was unaware of the affair at the time he called Kessler about Alice Huang’s detention in Singapore. But in the weeks following the call, BIS staff were muzzled in their ability to investigate the company, including a mandate that they route all request of Nvidia through Kessler, Bloomberg reported.

BIS spokespeople earlier denied any wrongdoing.

“It’s really important to understand what the Commerce Department knew about Megaspeed,” said Ben Buchanan, former White House special adviser for AI during the Biden administration, in a Bloomberg Television interview. “This is an incident where the enforcement is not good. The decision making has not been good.”

More stories like this are available on bloomberg.com

news.summary: Commerce chief under scrutiny over BIS actions and export-control gaps tied to Nvidia’s China ties, even as Trump pledges support and lawmakers prepare inquiries

news.title: Desire within US, India to conclude trade deal by G20: ex-US diplomat
news.text:
Washington: There is a desire within the US and India to try to conclude phase one of the bilateral trade agreement, perhaps by the G20 Summit in Florida next month, a former senior US diplomat said.India and the US finalised a framework for the first phase of the bilateral trade agreement in February following a phone call between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and US President Donald Trump. However, changes in the American tariff landscape have led to renewed negotiations, which are yet to conclude."By all expectations, I think that there's a desire to try to conclude the phase one deal, perhaps by the G20," Nisha Biswal, former Assistant Secretary of State for South and Central Asia, told PTI in an interview here.The G20 brings together major industrialised and developing economies to discuss global issues. Under a rotating presidency, it holds ministerial meetings throughout the year, culminating in an annual Leaders' Summit, which Trump will chair on December 14-15 in Florida, US.Biswal termed the ongoing trade talks as "complicated" and said that the negotiators have to work through certain areas, including the demand for comparative advantage made by New Delhi over its rivals in sectors such as textiles.Live Events"For the administration, trying to figure out how to address that and still stay within the strictures of the tools that it is using is also going to be an issue that they have to navigate," she said.Biswal said she was hopeful that Washington and New Delhi were aware of both the importance of the US-India corridor and the ability of the trade negotiators to actually reach an outcome."They are two extraordinarily complex economies. So I understand that this is not quite as easy as a back-of-the-envelope type of agreement; we're actually trying to get through a lot of tricky issues," she said.Biswal said the India-US relationship has been a mixed bag during President Trump's second tenure, which started in 2025.She said the bilateral relationship stabilised after Modi and Trump announced the framework of the first phase of the trade deal in February this year and negotiations began in earnest."2026, I think, saw a kind of stabilisation in the relationship as the trade negotiations kind of took off in earnest, particularly after India made some very smart moves," Biswal said.The former diplomat said the US took note when Prime Minister Modi met with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation meeting in Tianjin last year."When India and the EU signed their trade agreement, again, Washington took notice. You saw from US Trade Representative Ambassador Jamieson Greer, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, comments to that effect in terms of India-EU," Biswal said."Not soon thereafter, you saw some agreement in principle on a phase one, you know, deal between the US and India," Biswal said.On October 20, Trump said Washington and New Delhi were "pretty close" to reaching a trade deal, adding that the proposed pact would differ from earlier agreements.Speaking to reporters at the Oval Office, he said India wanted to make a deal and expressed confidence that an agreement would be reached.India's Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal on Thursday said New Delhi will have one of the "best" trade deals with Washington in every respect.He said that India has negotiated a very good set of outcomes with the US in the pact."And in every respect, India will have one of the best deals with the US," he told reporters in Visakhapatnam.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: Iran claims strike on US radar in Bahrain
news.text:
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has claimed to have struck a US early-warning radar installation in Bahrain.

In a statement carried by Iranian media on Friday, the IRGC said the attack was in retaliation for an alleged enemy airstrike on a telecommunications tower in Sirik, in Iran’s southern Hormozgan Province. The Guards claimed to have destroyed the radar, although neither the strike nor the reported damage has been independently verified.

There was no immediate confirmation from the US military or Bahrain.

The incident comes amid continued tensions between Washington and Tehran, with peace negotiations stalled and fears persisting over a possible resumption of major US military operations.

US President Donald Trump said on Monday that further military action against Iran did not appear necessary, expressing hope for a diplomatic breakthrough amid calls for restraint from Arab allies. However, he warned that US forces remained “locked and loaded” and ready to resume strikes if circumstances changed.

In a Truth Social post on Thursday, Trump declared that the US no longer needed a peace deal with Iran, claiming Washington controlled Iranian funds and the Strait of Hormuz.

The US carried out limited airstrikes against Iranian air-defense positions on Qeshm Island on November 2 and 6. Trump described the latest operation as “minor.” Media reports have said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pressed Trump to launch a new offensive against Iran following the November 3 US midterm elections, but the president declined.

Speaking to conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt on Thursday, Trump warned that Iran would “not exist very long” if it killed a senior US official. The remarks followed reports that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had moved to a military base over alleged Iranian threats, which Tehran denied.

Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, warned on Thursday that US military bases involved in any renewed attack on Iran, including those in Europe, would be considered legitimate targets. “No safe distance. No safe haven. No immunity,” he wrote on X.
news.summary:
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claim to have struck a US radar in Bahrain amid stalled peace talks and threats of renewed war

news.title: Japan warns defence contractors of potential cuts to military orders amid fiscal constraints: Report
news.text:
ReutersFinance ministry officials last week proposed spending between 50 trillion and 60 trillion yen ($313 billion to $376 billion) on defence over the five years starting in April 2027 (Representative Image)

Tokyo: Japan has warned defence contractors of deep cuts to expected orders as fiscal constraints threaten to scale back a military buildup that Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's government says is needed to counter China, four sources said.Finance ministry officials last week proposed spending between 50 trillion and 60 trillion yen ($313 billion to $376 billion) on defence over the five years starting in April 2027, the people familiar with the proposal told Reuters.That would exceed the current 43 trillion yen five-year plan but fall well short of the 80 trillion yen advocated by some defence officials and ruling Liberal Democratic Party lawmakers.Read more: Japan casts military buildup as path to economic prosperityThe gap could mean cuts by as much as half in planned purchases of some missiles and aircraft, including US-made F-35 stealth fighters, the sources said.Live EventsThe sources asked not to be identified because they were not authorised to speak to the media. The finance and defence ministries did not immediately respond to requests for comment.The revised spending proposal would leave Japan short of its target of raising defence outlays to 2% of gross domestic product, according to Reuters calculations, as US President Donald Trump presses Washington's allies to spend more on their militaries.The 2026 US National Defense Strategy calls for allies worldwide to spend 3.5% of GDP on their armed forces and a further 1.5% on broader security needs.Read more: Japan eyes Indian live firing ranges for missile and drone training as defence cooperation deepensSALES TAXFinance ministry officials argue that a steeper increase would be difficult to fund alongside Takaichi's commitments to invest in economic growth and cut the sales tax on food, which would squeeze government revenue, three of the sources said.The sales tax cut would leave an annual 4.3 trillion yen revenue shortfall that Takaichi would need to fill through other funding sources, potentially including foreign exchange reserves.The finance ministry's defence proposal, however, is likely to face resistance from security hawks in Takaichi's party, setting up a clash over how much Japan can afford to spend to bolster its defences."A contingency could occur at any time. If the goal is to build the capabilities necessary to deter and prevent such a contingency, a figure in the 50-trillion-yen range is out of the question," one ruling party official familiar with the discussions said, requesting anonymity because of the sensitivity of the issue.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: Trump threatens to double Mexico tariffs over migrant caravans
news.text:
Washington: US President Donald Trump on Thursday threatened to double tariffs on Mexico unless it can keep migrant caravans from reaching the common border, something the Mexican government has been regularly doing.

The Mexican government has intervened to block several groups of migrants traveling up from Central America since September, but at least two more groups have attempted the journey in recent days.

“Here we go again! With the perceived loss by the Republicans in the Midterms... the INVASION of our Country is taking place again,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.

“They will not be accepted! MEXICO MUST STOP THEM, NOW, and if they do not do so, the Tariffs on Mexico will be IMMEDIATELY DOUBLED.”

Members of the caravans, one with about 1,000 people and another numbering around 100, have told AFP they hoped that the midterm election defeat of Trump’s Republicans would result in less stringent US border restrictions.

Democrats swept both chambers of Congress and won the governorship of Texas for the first time in more than three decades.

Mexican security personnel intervened against the group of 100 people on Tuesday after they crossed a river separating Mexico from Guatemala, reportedly detaining dozens of people.

Two days earlier, however, the group of 1,000 people crossed into Mexico without encountering resistance. On Thursday, they were making their way across Mexico’s southern state of Chiapas, which borders Guatemala.

Another caravan is expected to leave Honduras on Sunday.

Mexico is Washington’s top trading partner, and the neighbors are currently renegotiating the terms of their free trade deal.

A large portion of the goods the United States imports from Mexico are not subject to tariffs, but steel and aluminum are subject to duties ranging from 25 percent to 50 percent.

‘No leniency!’

Such caravans were a frequent occurrence during Trump’s first term and during the administration of Joe Biden.

Since Trump’s return to office on a hard-line anti-immigration agenda, illegal border crossings have plummeted.

He has also heaped pressure on Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum to increase her country’s own efforts at impeding migrants from reaching the border.

“There will be no leniency!” Trump warned.

Sheinbaum said Thursday that since Trump’s return to the White House in January 2025, no migrant caravan had reached the US border.

“There are people who mislead migrants by saying, for instance, that the US election result has changed immigration policy, which is simply not true,” Sheinbaum said.

“We’re telling the people in the caravan that entering the United States is extremely difficult, and that if their goal is to reach the United States, they will not be able to do so,” she added.

“We are looking for ways to ensure they return to their home countries safely or, if someone wishes to remain in Mexico under specific conditions and in a designated location, that is also an option.”

The US State Department has revoked visas, or revoked the right to even apply for visas, from more than 15 people believed to be organizing migrant caravans.
news.summary: President Trump warned of increased tariffs on Mexico if migrant caravans are not curtailed. Mexico has attempted to block recent migrant groups heading from Central America.

news.title: What we know after Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO
news.text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned from his top post at the chipmaker he co-founded, after reports of the tech titan's extramarital affairs came into the spotlight this week.

One of those relationships has raised national security concerns. The New York Times reported that Huang had an affair with a businesswoman U.S. intelligence suspects to be a Chinese spy, which Beijing denies. Separately, the outlet and later others reported that Nvidia employees said Huang had another affair with an executive who reported to him directly — compounding calls for him to step down.

Nvidia announced Huang's resignation on Thursday, effective immediately. The California-based company said that Colette Kress — who has been Nvidia's chief financial officer and executive vice president since 2013 — will step into the role of interim CEO.

The scandal marks the most tumultuous chapter yet for Nvidia, whose high-end chips have emerged as the leading building blocks for artificial intelligence. Huang himself has become a key face in the AI race, both across the industry and often on U.S. President Donald Trump’s side in Washington.

Here's what we know.

 Nvidia's new leadership 

Nvidia said Kress is now interim CEO. Prior to joining Nvidia over 13 years ago, Kress worked at Cisco, Microsoft and Texas Instruments.

In a statement about her new post on Thursday, Kress said Nvidia’s “strength has always come from its people” and that she's “committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years.”

Huang co-founded Nvidia, alongside Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, back in 1993 — and until Thursday had led the company ever since, with no clear successor in sight. Huang's ouster has led to a scramble for a new permanent CEO, and Nvidia said it's considering both “internal and external candidates.”

The company's board of directors also said Thursday that it has named its first-ever chairman, Harvey C. Jones.

 Affairs in the spotlight 

Over the weekend, following news reports of Huang's relationship with a woman identified as former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, Nvidia's then-CEO apologized for being “unfaithful to my wife.”

"My actions hurt her and our children,” Huang wrote in a Sunday email to employees, adding that his colleagues also “deserve better” from him.

Neither Huang nor Nvidia identified who he had been intimate with by name, but the apology arrived shortly after Nvidia said it was investigating whether Huang had been “the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”

Last month, the Times reported that U.S. intelligence agencies discovered Nvidia’s Huang had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang, who also goes by the name Huang Le — and determined she was feeding information directly to Beijing. (Huang is a common surname and the two are not related).

Nvidia initially maintained Huang would stay on as CEO as the company conducted its investigation. But scrutiny grew late Wednesday after reports emerged that Huang had a separate affair with an Nvidia executive. Huang’s resignation arrived shortly after. The company didn't address either relationship in its Thursday announcement.

Later on Thursday, Reuters reported Huang had an intimate relationship with a second employee, citing unidentified sources.

 Where investigations stand 

Nvidia hasn't provided any notable new updates in its internal review announced Sunday. At the time, the company said it had “no reason to believe” that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, but that its inquiry would examine all available information.

Trump was reportedly briefed about intelligence findings involving Huang well before the scandal erupted publicly. But when asked over the weekend whether he wished he had acted sooner on that information, the president said “I don’t think so” and maintained that Nvidia’s CEO was an “honorable guy.”

Trump later said the FBI is looking into Huang's affair with Alice Huang, although where exactly that probe stands is unclear. Meanwhile, lawmakers from both sides of the aisle on Capitol Hill are calling for further investigations.

Many eyes have been on Nvidia’s ties to Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which prominently touts the companies’ partnership on its website. Last year, Megaspeed was accused of illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China, but in December said there was “no evidence” of such exports. 

On Thursday, Megaspeed maintained it takes its obligation to comply with American export control laws “extremely seriously" — and that it was committed to working “constructively and transparently” with the U.S. government.

Singaporean authorities said they questioned Alice Huang and confiscated her passport last year as part of an investigation into Megaspeed. They concluded there wasn’t enough evidence that she had committed a crime, but suspected she provided “inaccurate information” to downplay her role at Megaspeed.

Malaysia said Friday it was investigating whether any of the chips brought into Malaysia by Megaspeed or its Malaysian affiliate Speedmatrix had been reexported to other country.

China, meanwhile, has denied that it attempted to ensnare Jensen Huang. Its Foreign Ministry earlier this week called the spying allegations “unsubstantiated” and said they amount to a smear campaign against Beijing.

 Trump continues his praise for Huang 

Huang has maintained a close relationship to Trump throughout the Republican president’s second term in office. He’s successfully lobbied for looser AI regulation overall — including less strict limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China. And he's among tech CEOs who have dined at the White House, and even traveled on Air Force One.

Trump has called Huang “smart” and “amazing,” repeatedly insisting he join him on foreign trips. After news of his resignation broke on Thursday, the president maintained that Huang had “done a fantastic job.”

He also chimed in with his own recommendation for Nvidia's CEO seat: former chief executive of Apple Tim Cook, who has similarly remained in Trump's orbit over recent years.

“There is only one man to take his place,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform Thursday. “Legend replaces a Legend!”

Critics quickly decried Trump's comments. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said the Republican administration had “repeatedly undermined the free market economy” and that Thursday marked the latest example of “Donald Trump weighing in on behalf of his views connected to corporate America, as opposed to focusing on working class America.”

 A new test for the AI industry 

The shockwaves of Huang's exit stress just how few figures hold so much power the AI race. Nvidia is one of the world’s most valuable companies today — and Huang himself (often wearing his signature leather jacket) has risen to fame across the tech world.

Some analysts suspect the foreign intelligence allegations will strengthen calls in Washington for stricter export controls with China, which could in turn renew trade strains overall. Others have called it a watershed moment for Nvidia, the chipmaker that has long been seen as the crown jewel for powering AI. And questions of security risks facing the companies at the forefront of this technology are piling up.

Nvidia shares fell more than 4% by market close Thursday, after plummeting earlier in the day.

Stephanie Balaouras, group research director for Forrester, said Huang’s resignation from Nvidia isn’t just a test for the company but the AI boom as a whole.

“If Nvidia stabilizes quickly under new leadership, the AI infrastructure boom will have demonstrated resilience," she said. “If its stock, financing relationships, or ecosystem commitments remain under sustained pressure, that would add evidence to the fragile side of the AI bubble ledger.”

AP Writers Kelvin Chan, Chan Ho-him, Mae Anderson and Lisa Mascaro contributed.
news.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned from his top post at the chipmaker he co-founded, after reports of the tech titan’s extramarital affairs came into the spotlight this week
news.author: Wyatte Grantham-Philips

news.title: Calls for Nvidia probes, new chip export limits intensify
news.text:
The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday did little to quell bipartisan demands from Congress for an accounting of potential national security fallout from his affair with an alleged Chinese spy and talk of adding tougher chip export controls to the annual defense authorization bill. 

Huang admitted on Sunday to having an affair, and reports say that it was with Alice Huang, an executive at Singaporean tech company and Nvidia customer Megaspeed, whom the U.S. government believes spied for China, according to recent reports. The New York Times and Reuters reported he also had affairs with two Nvidia employees.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters Thursday that he supports the Senate investigating Huang’s potential influence on U.S. artificial intelligence and chip policy.

“I think that it would make sense because of the… nature of the association… and the governments and the national security interests we were talking about here,” Thune said, though he said he thought it would be “wrong” to make assumptions about how close Huang’s relationship with President Donald Trump has been.

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., echoed the need for lawmakers to delve into the scandal, saying in a post on X that “Congress must demand answers.”

“The Trump administration must also answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Were government officials told not to investigate because of Trump’s relationship with Mr. Huang? What did Trump know when he personally invited Mr. Huang aboard Air Force One?” Schumer wrote, referring to the president having invited Huang to accompany him to China in May. 

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said at a press conference that Reps. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., and Jim Himes, D-Conn., the ranking members of the Foreign Affairs and Intelligence committees, respectively, are leading Democrats’ efforts to “get to the bottom of what has happened.”

“We need a classified briefing made available to members of Congress as it relates to the Nvidia situation,” Jeffries said. “And to the extent that our national security has been compromised, the American people deserve answers, and we’re going to work to make sure that happens.”

The investigations look likely to begin before control of Congress changes hands in January.

Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., who chairs the House select China committee, told reporters that his panel, along with House Foreign Affairs and Intelligence, are in negotiations with Huang to find a date for his testimony before Congress.

“The bottom line is we need to understand the magnitude of this with respect to Chinese intelligence, possible chip diversion,” Moolenaar said. “What ways is Chinese intelligence influencing his perspective, his perspective influencing national security policy?”

Last week, the chairs of the three committees sent a letter to Huang requesting that he appear at a joint closed-door briefing. Moolenaar said that if Huang does not agree to a date, the committees will subpoena him.

Late Thursday, he joined with House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, R-Fla., and House Intelligence Chairman Rick Crawford, R-Ark., in sending a new letter to Huang seeking a closed-door transcribed interview on Dec. 1. They also wrote to Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter seeking a similar interview on Dec. 2. Separately, Mast wrote to Jeffrey Kessler, the Commerce Department undersecretary for industry and security, seeking his appearance at a committee hearing on Dec. 3.

Moolenaar also said that Congress needs to understand what privileged information Chinese intelligence may have gained access to through Huang and how they may have tried to influence U.S. policy.

“We need to have strong safeguards when it comes to our technology and export controls,” Moolenaar said. “And [Huang has] been one of the strongest proponents for not having export controls. This shines a whole new light on that discussion.”

NDAA outlook

A proposed manager’s amendment to the Senate’s fiscal 2027 National Defense Authorization Act bill (S 4784) contains several possibilities for those safeguards, including requirements for chip security mechanisms that would allow for verification if semiconductors are diverted to countries of concern and a ban on exporting certain very powerful chips to those countries. The House NDAA does not contain similar language.

However, House Armed Services Chair Mike D. Rogers, D-Ala., is open to the restrictions. He told reporters Wednesday that he “would like to see” semiconductor export controls in the NDAA, but that the Huang scandal had not changed his position.

Democratic Caucus Vice Chair Ted Lieu, D-Calif., told reporters on Thursday that after reports that the federal government had been aware of Huang’s affair with the alleged spy, the administration should have shared the information with Congress.

“The administration needs to be investigated for hiding this information from Congress and the American people,” he said.

Lieu also suggested that Nvidia’s reported donation to the White House ballroom project influenced the Trump administration’s decision to allow the export of some powerful Nvidia chips to China.

“There is no reason to do that. That hurts our national security, and we have an opportunity right now to fix that in the upcoming National Defense Authorization,” Lieu said.

Mast said the Huang revelations could give new momentum to including chip export rules in the NDAA. He also said that his “directive” on the issue came “straight from the admin” and informed his objectives on the committee.

“Don’t let chips be smuggled to China. Make sure that American companies get to buy them first,” Mast said. “Make sure that the machines that make them don’t get sold to them, even though it’s the Dutch that make the machines. Make sure that they can’t access it remotely.”

Mast’s committee has advanced many of those priorities, including some of the language included in the NDAA.

In March, the committee on a unanimous vote advanced legislation known as the Chip Security Act, which would require chip security mechanisms to verify that certain semiconductors subject to export controls aren’t diverted to countries of concern, including China and Iran.

The committee also advanced bills to require the Bureau of Industry and Security and the State Department to work with allied suppliers of semiconductor manufacturing equipment to implement export controls to prevent the equipment from going to countries of concern, and to require licenses for the export of certain powerful chips, including banning exporting certain chips to countries of concern.

Versions of all three bills are included in the Senate manager’s amendment to the NDAA.

Lutnick focus

The scandal has also led to calls for oversight of the Commerce Department, including Secretary Howard Lutnick, for its handling of export policy and actions around Huang.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., told reporters Thursday that Lutnick and Nvidia should testify “before Democrats can set the narrative.”

“If there is some reasonable basis or some way to discount some of the reporting, the best way to do it is request a meeting with us and give us a briefing,” Tillis said. “Because otherwise, you’re going to get what you get in an oversight hearing in about six weeks.”

Asked about oversight of the Commerce Department’s role in the Huang scandal, Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, who chairs the Commerce Committee, said his panel “has engaged in vigorous oversight under Republican presidents and Democrat presidents and will continue to be [engaged in it].”

On Wednesday, prior to Huang’s resignation, Senate Banking ranking member Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., and Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller requesting that they “preserve all documents, communications, records, and other materials regarding the export of NVIDIA’s advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China.”

“This incident raises significant concerns about the federal government’s ability to effectively enforce our export controls and protect our national security,” the senators wrote.

In a statement Thursday, Warren said that Huang’s resignation did not “absolve” him of the need to answer questions. She also called for the passage of stricter export controls, including the bill to ban the export of certain chips to China.

Sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., sent his own letter on Wednesday to Lutnick, Rubio, Attorney General Todd Blanche and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, requesting an update on the Justice Department’s investigation into Megaspeed for possibly diverting U.S. chips to China.

Savannah Behrmann, John M. Donnelly, Jacob Fulton and David Jordan contributed to this report.

news.title: Delusional Trump, 80, Teases New War Since He’s ‘More Popular Now’
news.text:
Donald Trump has teased launching a new war before his presidency ends, claiming his popularity has grown among a key voting bloc.”

Trump, 80, has repeatedly suggested that an American intervention in Cuba could happen under his watch, but set a deadline for his plans during a Thursday interview with conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt on Salem News Channel.

“I want to get Cuba done before I leave,” Trump told Hewitt.

He added that Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s parents are from Cuba, “So he would love to do that.”

“I would like to be able to do it,” Trump continued, then claimed, “I won the Cuban vote by 94 percent in Florida, and I think I’m more popular now than I was then.”

Trump also made the 94 percent claim on Monday, saying, “We have tremendous people who were treated very badly, Cuban Americans, and they voted for me 94 percent, and we take care of those people.”

Back in April, Trump said, “We have a lot of great Cuban Americans, all of whom just about voted for me.

It is not clear where Trump’s figure is pulled from. He won 68 percent of the Cuban American vote in Florida in the 2024 presidential election.

Florida was one of the few states to buck the blue wave in the midterms, with two Trump allies elected, congressman Byron Donalds as governor and Ashley Moody to the U.S. Senate.

The Daily Beast has contacted the White House for comment.

Despite Trump’s claim of his improving popularity in Florida, his administration’s brutal ICE raids have seen some Cuban Americans who voted for him turn against him.

Cuban-born immigration lawyer Ismael Labrador told News in America last week that he was dismayed by the surge in people seeking his legal services amid the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

“We have relatives living in fear right now, we’ve had relatives who have been deported back to Cuba, unfortunately,” Labrador said.

While he voted for Trump, he admitted he was “blindsided” by the administration.

“Personally, I voted for Trump because I wanted to get criminals out of the country,” he said.

“We wanted to have a safe America. We never thought that he was going to go after everybody. This isn’t what I voted for.”

In September, Republican Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, who has held a Miami seat since 2021, posted a video that said, “Mr. president, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far.”

She added, “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.”

During Thursday’s interview, Hewitt asked Trump if he would be comfortable with the use of “a little bit” of military force to free Cuba from its communist regime, with the president admitting he “would certainly consider that.”

Trump said in March he believed he would have the “honor” of taking over Cuba.

“I think I can do anything I want with it,” he said at the time. “Whether I free it, take it, I think I can do anything I want with it.”

Despite declaring himself the “president of peace,” in his second term, Trump launched a war with Iran in February that has seen the price of oil soar globally.

He also oversaw a raid in Venezuela to capture leader Nicolas Maduro and the U.S. has taken military action against Houthi rebels in Yemen, as well as strikes in Syria and Iraq.

Trump, 80, has repeatedly suggested that an American intervention in Cuba could happen under his watch, but set a deadline for his plans during a Thursday interview with conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt on Salem News Channel.

“I want to get Cuba done before I leave,” Trump told Hewitt.

Read more at The Daily Beast.
