news.title: Trump threatens Mexico with doubled tariffs as nearly 2,000 migrants head towards US border
news.text: 18d561d9-1626-418d-a213-ac97c88598d9 Washington DC Nearly 2,000 migrants from Central and South America are heading towards the US southern border following the Democrats' gains in the midterm elections, with US President Donald Trump threatening to immediately double tariffs on Mexico if it fails to stop the caravan from reaching American territory. In a post on Truth Social on Thursday (local time), Trump linked the formation of new migrant caravans to the Republicans' performance in the midterm elections, claiming that the movement was taking place following the party's electoral losses. He said, "Here we go again! With the perceived loss by the Republicans in the Midterms - I was not on the ballot- the invasion of our Country is taking place again. Huge caravans are forming and beginning their illegal march through Mexico. Many of the people in these Caravans are those that various countries don’t want - “Send them to America,” they say - But they will not be accepted!” He warned, "Mexico must stop them now, and if they do not do so, the Tariffs on Mexico will be immediately doubled. Mexico, the Governor of Texas, the very liberal new Governor of Texas, our great Border Patrol & ICE, have been so informed. There will be no leniency! Thank you for your attention to this matter." Fox News reported that migrants travelling with the caravan expected the Democrats to welcome them and provide opportunities to build new lives in the United States. One migrant told Fox News, "We are seeing it this way because we know that the Democrats are not going to let a point as big as the Latino vote be lost. And I think they are going to give us the opportunity to reach our new homes and our new opportunities." The developments come as the Democrats' midterm gains are expected to have implications for immigration enforcement, including legal challenges to state-level measures targeting illegal immigration. According to Fox News, Democratic state attorneys general-elect could withdraw legal defences of certain Republican-backed immigration laws after taking office, potentially affecting ongoing court proceedings. In Texas, Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson could drop the state's defence of SB4, a Republican-backed law that allows state authorities to arrest and prosecute people suspected of illegally crossing the US-Mexico border. The New Orleans-based Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals allowed the law to take effect in April while a legal challenge against it proceeds. However, current Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton will remain in office until Johnson is sworn in on January 1, 2027. Paxton had opted not to seek re-election to the post while pursuing an unsuccessful Senate bid.Meanwhile, Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier criticised Democratic efforts to loosen immigration enforcement, defending the state's existing approach. "I don't think we can entertain amnesty in a conversation," Uthmeier told "The Will Cain Show" on Wednesday evening (local time), as reported by Fox News. "We have to be a country focused on the rule of law. In Florida we've deported a record number, tens of thousands of criminal illegal aliens, child predators, murderers, people who have committed violent crimes, and we're at an all-time crime low. We're safer than ever after shutting down the border," he added. In another legal development, the US Supreme Court is weighing whether to take up Iowa's appeal of a ruling blocking a state law that would allow officials to arrest and prosecute people residing in the country illegally.Fox News reported that Iowa Attorney General-elect Nate Willems could choose not to defend the law if the Supreme Court takes up the case.
news.summary: Nearly 2,000 migrants head to the US border as Trump warns of Mexico tariffs if the caravan advances, fueling immigration and policy tensions

news.title: Trump Threatens Iran With Military Strikes If US Officials Are Targeted
news.text: US President Donald Trump on Thursday (local time) warned Iran of severe consequences if Tehran targets American officials, saying those responsible "will not exist any longer", while asserting that he would not hesitate to use military force if the situation takes an unfavourable turn.In a phone interview with Salem News Channel, Trump was asked what Washington would do if Iran killed a US official, such as Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent."They will not exist any longer," Trump responded, issuing a stark warning to Tehran.The remarks came after Bessent reportedly moved from his residence in Washington, DC, to a US military base earlier this week following alleged threats to his life from Iran.Trump also said he would consider it a defeat if Iran's current leadership remained in power when he leaves office.Asked whether it would amount to a failure if the "Iran crazies" were still ruling the country at the end of his presidency, Trump replied, "Yes, that would be a defeat.""Yep, I would say that would be a defeat. Absolutely," he added.Addressing the possibility of further military action against Iran, Trump said he had no hesitation about using force to prevent Tehran from threatening US allies and maritime interests.When asked whether he would hesitate to use military force to stop Iran from "terrorising our allies and our ships", Trump said, "No hesitation."He further claimed that the United States was making progress in its operations against Iran and said Washington was extracting more oil than before the conflict began."We're doing very well with it right now, we're taking out more oil now than we did before the, if you call it a war, before the war started. news.title: Chuck Schumer Faces Senate Majority Challenger as Van Hollen Enters Race
news.text: Maryland U.S. Senator Chris Van Hollen said Thursday that he will run for Senate majority leader in the next Congress, setting up a challenge against Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer after the party swept to power in the midterm elections. Van Hollen's announcement Thursday makes him the first to challenge New York's Schumer. “In this election, the American people called for change,” Van Hollen said in a statement. He argued that voters rejected President Donald Trump’s policies and that “the status quo that isn’t working for working people.” Democrats need new leadership to answer voters’ demands, he added. Van Hollen called it “a generational opportunity for the Senate to respond to the call of the American people for change." Pressure for a challenge had been building since Election Day. Former presidential candidate and progressive Senator Bernie Sanders is among the highest-profile voices criticizing the New York lawmaker's direction, but several Democratic centrists have also declined to back Schumer for the role he has held since 2017. Schumer has said he expects to keep his job and declined to directly answer a question about whether he has spoken to Van Hollen since he began mulling a challenge. Earlier this week, he told reporters, “I’ll be reelected as majority leader.” His allies point to the midterm results. New York Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, who ran Senate Democrats’ campaign arm this cycle, said that Schumer not only won the Senate back but he “cares deeply, and he understands politics well." Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed has repeatedly said he would support Maryland's Van Hollen for the majority leader role. Connecticut Senator Richard Blumenthal also said he was open to new leadership if a challenger stepped forward. Van Hollen has served in the Senate since 2017 and previously spent 14 years in the House. Senate Democrats will likely hold elections next month for their top positions. Schumer’s reelection requires a majority of caucus votes to succeed. Newsweek has reached out to the offices of Schumer and Van Hollen for comment. news.summary: Maryland U.S. Senator Chris Van Hollen said Thursday that he will run for Senate majority leader in the next Congress.

news.title: 'I'm A Piece Of Sh*t': Inside Jensen Huang's Final Hours As Nvidia CEO
news.text: At the end, Jensen Huang looked broken and shattered, his legendary energy depleted. After weeks spent denying the allegations of infidelity and fighting to remain in his job as Nvidia Corp.'s chief executive officer, his surrender late Wednesday night was unconditional. Huang's usual take-charge demeanor had evaporated, according to a person familiar with the situation, and he'd started using phrases like "whatever" and "I don't care." For the decades he spent building Nvidia into a multitrillion-dollar AI chip behemoth, Huang was famous for his attention to the tiniest of details, from chip architecture to the compensation packages of even the most junior employees at the company. Now, in the eyes of the people in the room, he had given up. According to people who've spoken with him in recent days, Huang has already taken a penitent turn, castigating himself as a "piece of sh--."It was a stunningly quick fall for a billionaire and tech titan who two weeks ago was the face of artificial intelligence around the world. With his directness and vigor, he had charmed US President Donald Trump, shaped global tech policy and drawn adoring crowds on his papal-style international tours. It's hard to imagine the current AI boom happening without Huang, his company and their chips, and it's hard to imagine what it will look like after his fall. As Harvey Jones, chair of the company's board of directors, wrote in an email to employees after Huang's ouster, "Jensen's contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world."Huang couldn't be reached for comment. When the news broke in late October that Huang had close ties with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, it looked like he would prevail. The board of directors, dominated by longtime investors, business partners and friends of Huang's, was reluctant to act on the news stories, or even publicly comment on them.Most of the news coverage tiptoed around the exact nature of the CEO's relationship with Alice Huang, the suspected spy. Huang denied to friends and colleagues that he had been unfaithful to his wife. He'd been denying it when questioned internally since late 2025. In one of his last interviews as CEO, Huang told Bloomberg News that his relationship with Alice Huang was typical of those with Chinese customers and executives. "It was all completely normal and not unusual," he said. Nvidia's headquarters in Santa Clara, California. Photo Credit: BloombergA turning point came last Friday, Nov. 6, when a Financial Times story cited US officials saying that the relationship had been a romantic one. Soon afterward, Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter went to Huang's house to confront him, and Huang confessed. At that point, most of the board still didn't want to take a public stance, but Teter, who is secretary of the board, told them they had to act. The board announced that they would investigate the allegations. A prominent law firm, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, would lead the inquiry. On Sunday, Huang emailed the entire company, admitting to the affair, apologizing to his family and vowing to "cooperate fully" with the board's investigation.As the scandal ballooned, there was evidence that it was, perhaps unsurprisingly, drawing Huang's attention away from his extensive duties at the company. As part of Nvidia's idiosyncratic org chart, Huang had around 60 executives at the company who reported to him, a small army by normal management standards. The whole company had to file emails with their top five priorities, which Huang used to check that everyone was working on what he considered most important. Normally he responded to them immediately at all hours of the day and night. In recent days the response times had grown longer. On Wednesday, the New York Times reported that Huang was also having an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care. This time, the board acted quickly. Directors assembled remotely on Wednesday, and the meeting lasted late into the night. In the end, Huang was given no choice but to resign, leaving him with no formal role at the company he co-founded. The next morning, the board announced Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress would step in as interim CEO. She was quick to try and reassure rattled employees. "I believe deeply in this company and in its future," Kress wrote in an email reviewed by Bloomberg. "More than anything, I believe in each of you, in our customers and partners and in the vital role we play every day in the global economy. The Board, staff and I recognize that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period and I want you to know how grateful we are for your resilience, professionalism and continued dedication. Thank you."She pledged to hold an all-hands meeting on Nov. 18. A day earlier, Nvidia is due to report results and disclose what Wall Street analysts predict will be a near doubling of quarterly sales growth.Now, the board confronts the difficult challenge of finding a replacement for Huang. Some executives considered likely to end up on the shortlist: Advanced Micro Devices Inc. CEO Lisa Su and Arm Holdings Plc CEO Rene Haas. It's hard to imagine anyone filling all his roles - technologist, executive, marketer, lobbyist, mascot - and the company never bothered to create a traditional succession plan. For better or worse, Nvidia will begin to look more like a regular company going forward, managed in a more regular way. As for Huang himself, he won't be able to retreat from public life, even if he wants to. In the coming weeks he's expected to testify before Congress, where politicians will ask him about his relationship with Alice Huang and whether it might have put some of the secrets of Nvidia's state-of-the-art chips at risk. In recent days, Huang has claimed not to care what happens to himself at this point, according to the people who've spoken with him. His main concern, he says, is his wife, and not "ruining the lives" of the multiple women now romantically linked to him in the public imagination.(This story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)
news.summary: For the decades Jensen Huang spent building Nvidia into a multitrillion-dollar AI chip behemoth.

news.title: India-US Relations at Crossroads: Why Trump’s Midterm Rebuke Will Not Resolve Fundamental Differences Over Strategic Interests and Security
news.text:
The strategic partnership between India and the United States is facing a growing test of trust as President Donald Trump’s America First foreign policy increasingly exposes differences over trade, energy security, Russia, China, Pakistan and Kashmir. Despite Washington’s repeated declarations about the importance of New Delhi, India is becoming increasingly concerned that its strategic interests are being subordinated to American commercial and political priorities.

At a recent Freedom 250 reception in Mumbai, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio described the relationship between the two countries as “defining, in many ways”. His remarks reflected Washington’s ambition to maintain India as a major strategic partner in the Indo-Pacific. However, the contradictions surrounding the Trump administration’s foreign policy have raised questions about whether the rhetoric is matched by a genuine willingness to accommodate India’s security and economic concerns.

The political setback suffered by Trump in the US midterm elections has added another dimension to the relationship. By handing control of both chambers of Congress to the Democrats, American voters have delivered a significant rebuke to the president’s domestic and foreign policy agenda, potentially limiting his ability to advance his priorities during the remainder of his presidency.

For India, however, the central question extends beyond Trump’s political fortunes. New Delhi must determine whether the transactional approach adopted by his administration represents a temporary presidential preference or a more permanent shift in America’s understanding of strategic partnerships.

Rubio’s recent visit to India offered an indication of Washington’s immediate priorities. His engagements visibly emphasized energy, investment and commercial cooperation. Discussions with Reliance Industries leadership focused on energy, data centres and business opportunities, while his visit to the Jamnagar refinery highlighted its capacity to process Venezuelan crude.

These engagements are important to bilateral economic relations. However, the prominence of commercial discussions, alongside relatively less visible political and strategic engagement, has reinforced concerns that Washington increasingly views its relationship with India through an economic rather than a comprehensive strategic lens.

The economic relationship itself remains unsettled. The much-anticipated India-US trade agreement continues to face difficulties, with disagreements over tariffs, market access and sensitive sectors, particularly agriculture. Conflicting statements from ministers on both sides regarding the progress of negotiations suggest that the proposed agreement remains far from completion.

Immigration policy has created another source of friction. The Trump administration’s crackdown on immigration, uncertainty surrounding H-1B visas and controversial deportations of Indian nationals in restraints have generated considerable unease in New Delhi.

India acknowledges the need to address illegal migration and cooperate with Washington on immigration enforcement. However, it expects Indian citizens to be treated with dignity and their legal rights respected.

The contradiction is particularly striking given the importance of Indian professionals to the American technology industry. Indian engineers, researchers and skilled workers have played a significant role in building the United States’ technology ecosystem. Yet increasingly restrictive immigration policies threaten to make their professional mobility more uncertain.

More consequential disagreements, however, concern India’s fundamental strategic interests, particularly its relations with Russia, China and Pakistan, as well as the Kashmir issue.

Washington’s approach to India’s energy relationship with Russia has become one of the clearest examples of the transactional nature of Trump’s foreign policy.

The United States has repeatedly criticised India’s purchases of Russian oil, arguing that revenues from energy exports help finance Moscow’s war against Ukraine. The Trump administration has also imposed punitive tariffs to pressure New Delhi into reducing its dependence on Russian energy.

For India, however, Russian oil purchases are primarily a matter of energy security, economic stability and affordability. As one of the world’s largest energy-consuming economies, India must maintain access to reliable and competitively priced supplies to support its growing industrial and transportation sectors.

The apparent double standard became more visible after Reuters reported on October 23 that a shipment of Russian diesel was heading towards New York following an arrangement between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The development raised questions in India about Washington’s selective approach to economic engagement with Moscow. When American consumers face higher fuel prices, the Trump administration appears willing to explore arrangements involving Russian energy. Yet India faces economic penalties and diplomatic pressure when it makes similar calculations based on its domestic requirements.

For New Delhi, the issue is not simply about Russian oil. It concerns the principle that strategic autonomy and national economic priorities should be respected in bilateral relations.

The contradictions are equally evident in Washington’s China policy.

Trump has pursued high-level engagement with Chinese President Xi Jinping, with their September 2026 Washington summit seeking to manage trade disputes and broader bilateral tensions despite continuing strategic competition.

Washington recognises that China is too economically powerful and deeply integrated into global supply chains to be managed exclusively through confrontation. Negotiations and pragmatic engagement remain essential elements of American policy towards Beijing.

India, however, faces a different set of expectations. While the United States retains considerable flexibility in managing its relationship with China, New Delhi is frequently expected to accommodate American demands concerning Russia and broader Indo-Pacific security priorities.

This creates an uncomfortable strategic imbalance.

India recognises the importance of preventing Chinese hegemony in Asia and shares several concerns with Washington regarding Beijing’s expanding military and economic influence. Nevertheless, it has never intended to become an instrument of American containment policy.

New Delhi has its own territorial dispute with China, continuing security concerns along the Line of Actual Control and independent calculations regarding regional stability. Its foreign policy cannot be subordinated to Washington’s strategic objectives.

The fundamental difference is that the United States wants the strategic advantages of India’s geographical position, military capabilities and regional influence without necessarily accepting corresponding security commitments. India, meanwhile, expects Washington to understand that its partnership must accommodate Indian interests and strategic priorities.

The Kashmir issue illustrates another important divergence.

India does not expect Washington to resolve the dispute. Its principal expectation is that the United States respects New Delhi’s longstanding position that India-Pakistan disputes should be addressed bilaterally, without external mediation.

Trump’s repeated claims of having mediated the May 2025 ceasefire between India and Pakistan therefore generated considerable discomfort in New Delhi. Such statements challenge India’s diplomatic position and raise questions about Washington’s willingness to respect its stated preferences on sensitive bilateral issues.

At the same time, the United States is unlikely to abandon its diplomatic flexibility towards Pakistan. Washington continues to have regional, military and counterterrorism interests that influence its engagement with Islamabad.

The contradiction is evident: Washington seeks flexibility in its approach to Kashmir and Pakistan while expecting greater conformity from India on Russia and other strategic matters.

American military cooperation with Pakistan has further complicated the relationship.

Washington’s proposed $686 million package to modernise Pakistan’s F-16 fighter fleet has revived longstanding Indian concerns about the military implications of American support for Islamabad.

India’s Defence Minister Rajnath Singh raised the issue directly with US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth during their meeting in Cebu on October 28.

Yet the same meeting also saw both countries reaffirm their ten-year defence cooperation framework. Hegseth reiterated Washington’s support for India against terrorism emanating from across its borders.

This juxtaposition captures the complexity of the bilateral relationship. The two countries are expanding defence cooperation while maintaining different assessments of regional security priorities.

For Washington, assistance to Pakistan may represent a separate tactical calculation. For New Delhi, however, American military support cannot be separated from Pakistan’s strategic relationship with China and the broader security environment in South Asia.

Indian External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar’s pointed observation at the G20 Foreign Ministers’ meeting in Atlanta that “tactical calculations should not lead to overlooking the dangers of terrorism” was an unmistakable reminder of this disconnect.

Despite its frustrations, India cannot afford to dismiss its relationship with the United States. Its own strategic vulnerabilities constrain its diplomatic choices.

Dependence on imported energy, Russian-origin military equipment and Western technology limits India’s room for manoeuvre. China’s economic weight, expanding military capabilities and influence across South Asia further complicate New Delhi’s strategic calculations.

India needs American investment, advanced technology, defence cooperation and access to global markets. At the same time, it cannot replace dependence on one external power with another.

Consequently, New Delhi has pursued a policy of diversification. It is strengthening domestic defence manufacturing, expanding technological capabilities, diversifying energy supplies and cultivating partnerships with Europe, Japan and other strategic partners.

These efforts reflect India’s determination to preserve strategic autonomy rather than align completely with any single power. However, building domestic industrial capacity and reducing external dependencies will require considerable time and investment.

The larger lesson from Rubio’s visit is that strategic importance does not automatically translate into diplomatic consideration. India remains a significant partner in American Indo-Pacific calculations, but the Trump administration’s commercial interests, domestic political priorities and transactional approach increasingly influence the relationship.

This does not mean the India-US partnership has failed. Both countries continue to share important interests in defence, technology, maritime security, trade and regional stability. Nevertheless, their expectations of the partnership are not always aligned, and the absence of a fully shared strategic vision is becoming increasingly apparent.

Rubio’s description of the relationship as defining for the 21st century reflects an ambitious vision. But a strategic partnership cannot become defining simply because Washington declares it so.

For India, the challenge is not merely to navigate the remaining years of Trump’s presidency. It must prepare for a relationship with the United States in which certain strategic priorities and policy expectations may continue beyond a single administration.

Washington, in turn, must recognise that India can be a consequential strategic partner without becoming a subordinate one.

The future of the relationship will ultimately depend on whether both countries can move beyond transactional calculations and develop a framework based on mutual respect, strategic sensitivity and trust. The United States may want greater alignment from India, but the durability of the partnership will depend on how seriously Washington is prepared to accommodate India’s independent interests.

news.text: US President Donald Trump on Thursday (local time) said former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was "going through hell" amid the controversy surrounding his alleged extramarital relationships, adding that the former technology executive was particularly distressed over the impact of the developments on his wife and family.Speaking in an interview with commentator Stephen A Smith, Trump said Huang had personally spoken to him and expressed regret over the situation involving his family."I spoke to him yesterday. He's going through hell. What he feels most badly about is his wife and family. That's what he is really, that's what he told me. And in, strongest, he called me as the president. I'm president, and he called me. And he said, what I've done to my wife and family is, that's what he talked about," Trump said.Trump added that he had always considered Huang a fine person and expressed confidence that the former Nvidia chief would eventually recover from the controversy."I know him pretty well. I always thought of him as a fine man," Trump said.The US President also questioned whether Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman alleged to have links to Chinese intelligence, was actually a spy, saying the matter had yet to be established.When asked whether Huang should have stepped down from his position, Trump said the woman's alleged intelligence links should have been a key consideration."Well, the big thing is, was the woman a spy? And I don't know if that's been determined yet," Trump said."But if the woman was a spy, yes. If the woman was not a spy, perhaps it would be different. But I can tell you this: somehow, he'll end up on his feet," he added.Trump's remarks came after Nvidia announced that its co-founder had stepped down as CEO following 33 years at the helm of the chipmaking giant, which he established in 1993.The controversy centres partly on Alice Huang, whose alleged links to Chinese intelligence have reportedly drawn attention within the US intelligence community. Jensen Huang had acknowledged having an extramarital relationship, with reports identifying Alice Huang as one of the women involved. The two are not related.China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs has dismissed allegations that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy as "groundless speculation and an attempt to smear and malign China."Separately, reports have also alleged that Huang had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, raising questions about potential workplace conflicts of interest.Trump's latest remarks appeared to differ from his comments on Monday, when he described Alice Huang as a spy and said Jensen Huang had denied knowing about her alleged intelligence links."I asked him that question, 'did you have any idea that she was a spy?' He said, 'I had no idea that she was a spy.' And I really believe him," Trump had said.Meanwhile, Trump reiterated his suggestion that former Apple CEO Tim Cook could take over Nvidia's leadership."I think Tim Cook would be a great candidate to run Nvidia," he told Smith.Earlier, during an interview with Salem News Channel, Trump had described Huang's departure as a "horrible thing" and said it was "so sad to see happen."Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and led its transformation into one of the world's leading suppliers of artificial intelligence chips. The company's board has appointed Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO while it considers a permanent successor.

news.title: Who Will Be Nvidia's Next CEO? Ian Buck, Colette Kress Lead Race as Trump Pushes Tim Cook to Replace Huang
news.text: Nvidia Corp. has begun searching for a new chief executive after co-founder Jensen Huang's sudden resignation. A wide field of potential successors is emerging, ranging from longtime insiders to rival chip executives and a surprise suggestion from President Donald Trump.Nvidia's board said Thursday it is "initiating a search for a permanent Chief Executive Officer and will consider internal and external candidates." Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress is serving as interim CEO and will remain CFO until a permanent successor is named.Huang, who never publicly named a successor, resigned as president, CEO and director following reports of two extramarital relationships, including one with a woman U.S. officials suspect of being a Chinese spy.Nvidia shares closed Thursday at $166.19, down 4.34%, after falling more than 11% earlier in the day. The stock hit a new 52-week low before paring losses.Trump backs Tim CookTrump weighed in on the search Thursday with a post on Truth Social."NOW THAT Nvidia CEO JENSEN HUANG, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place - TIM COOK of Apple," Trump wrote. "A Legend replaces a Legend!"Cook, who led Apple for nearly 15 years before John Ternus took over as CEO on Sept. 1, has not commented on Trump's suggestion. On prediction market Polymarket, traders ranked Cook behind Ian Buck, Kress and Arm CEO Rene Haas.Trump later described the Huang saga as a "horrible thing" and "so sad to see," CNBC reported.The insidersMany analysts and investors see two Nvidia executives as particularly likely candidates, at least in the short term: Kress and Buck, Reuters reported.Colette Kress, Nvidia's CFO since 2013, previously worked at Microsoft, Cisco and Texas Instruments. She is the executive most familiar to investors after Huang."Colette has helped lead NVIDIA through a period of extraordinary growth and has a deep understanding of our business, customers, operations and financial position," said Harvey C. Jones, whom the board named as its first-ever chair.Analysts see Kress as a steady choice for a crisis. Citi analysts Atif Malik and Papa Sylla wrote that she could serve as interim CEO while the board evaluates outside candidates, CNBC reported.Ian Buck, Nvidia's vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, joined the company in 2004. He helped lead development of CUDA, the software platform that made Nvidia chips the standard for AI. He now manages Nvidia's AI hardware and software products for its largest customers.Polymarket traders initially favored Buck as the most likely next CEO, although trading volume on that market was small.Some investors have suggested a shared leadership structure. Armina Rosenberg of Minotaur Capital suggested pairing "one leader to steady the business and the finances, such as Colette Kress, alongside a product and technology leader, such as Ian Buck."The outsidersSeveral executives at other major tech companies have also been mentioned.Rene Haas, CEO of chip designer Arm Holdings, is the outside candidate with the most support in media reports. Haas spent seven years at Nvidia, where he ran its computing products business, before joining Arm in 2013. He became Arm's CEO in 2022 and led its 2023 Nasdaq listing.A chips banker told Reuters that Haas made the most "logical sense." Shay Boloor, chief market strategist at Futurum Equities, also said Haas could be an outside candidate worth considering.Lisa Su, CEO of rival Advanced Micro Devices, has also been named in reports. Like Huang, Su was born in Taiwan. Hiring the chief of Nvidia's closest competitor, however, would be highly unusual.Other names floated include Micron Technology CEO Sanjay Mehrotra, Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji, Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman, Google AI infrastructure leader Amin Vahdat, Marvell Technology CEO Matt Murphy and former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger.None of the reported candidates has publicly commented on the Nvidia job.A hard act to followAnalysts say replacing Huang will be difficult. He co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and built it into a company worth more than $4 trillion."My bigger concern is next decade, because Jensen isn't simply Nvidia's CEO but he's the person who has consistently identified where computing is going," Boloor told Reuters.Investors want a leader who understands the technology, has a long-term vision and has strong financial skills, according to Reuters.Bernstein on Thursday cut its price target on Nvidia in half, to $200 from $400.Bloomberg reported that Nvidia is working with an outside search firm to identify candidates. The board did not give a timeline for naming a permanent CEO.Kress' first major test will come Tuesday, Nov. 17, when Nvidia reports fiscal third-quarter results.This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute investment advice.

news.title: India bond selloff may continue as Treasury rout, fresh debt sale hurt
news.text: MUMBAI Indian government bonds are likely to face selling pressure in early trades on Friday as a selloff in US Treasuries persists, while traders brace for heavy debt supply of the benchmark paper in the weekly auction later in the day. The benchmark 6.94 per cent 2036 bond yield is expected to move between 7.23 per cent and 7.28 per cent, according to a private-bank trader, after ending at 7.2467 per cent on Thursday. New Delhi plans to sell ₹34,000 crore ($3.62 billion) of the benchmark 2036 paper later in the day, taking its outstanding issuance to ₹2.72 lakh crore, the highest for any security ever. “We should see some caution at bidding, and any major moves would be seen only after the cutoffs,” the trader said. US Treasury yields rose on Thursday after US President Donald Trump said the US does not need a deal with Iran, as traders weighed the chance of a larger-than-usual Federal Reserve rate hike next month. October consumer-price data has beaten forecasts, spurring traders to ramp up bets on a larger rate increase on December 9. The 10-year US yield comfortably broke above the 5 per cent handle on Thursday and stayed higher in Asian hours, as traders have now assigned a 15 per cent probability to a larger-than-expected 50-basis-point rate hike, up from zero just a week ago. Elevated oil prices have also added to concerns about inflation, which has run above the Fed’s 2 per cent target for almost six years. Back home, India’s annual retail inflation accelerated to 6.09 per cent in October from 5.54 per cent in September, which was above an estimate of 5.93 per cent in a Reuters poll. The Reserve Bank of India, which raised its key rate in October for the first time in nearly four years, is expected to deliver another hike in early December. Rates Overnight index swap rates may continue to move higher in line with Treasury yields. The 1-year, 2-year and 5-year OIS rates rose 4 to 5 basis points to 6.44 per cent, 6.43 per cent and 6.53 per cent, respectively, on Thursday.

news.title: What’s next for Ukraine-Russia peace talks as war approaches fifth year?
news.text:
U.S. envoys met Thursday with Russian President Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin before heading to Ireland for talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky as Washington sought new momentum for its peace efforts.

Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who is also President Donald Trump's son-in-law, brokered talks this week between delegations from Moscow and Kyiv. 

The session in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, brought the first direct discussions between Ukrainian and Russian representatives in nine months as the push for a settlement stalled.

The talks produced no major breakthrough, aside from an agreement to swap a large number of prisoners, with the exact figure still to be announced. 

Plans for another round of talks were announced as well, with Witkoff and Zelensky saying Europe will join, though they gave no details about which countries or how many.

Kushner and Witkoff met with Putin for about two hours before going to Dublin, where they met with Zelensky for more than an hour as the conflict stretches toward the five-year mark.

Kushner said one goal of the meeting with Putin was to get the Russian leader’s blessing for European representatives to be part of the talks, which are looking at the continent’s broader security arrangements.

In Abu Dhabi, several European security advisers were involved on the sidelines but not in the main three-way talk.

Speaking to reporters before boarding a plane to leave Moscow, Witkoff said the next round of talks has been agreed upon.

Russian state TV showed Witkoff saying that “the Europeans will join at the next meeting,” but he did not elaborate.

Zelensky in Dublin indicated the Europeans would not be on the sidelines. 

“Next meeting, Europe will be during negotiations, will be a negotiation team – not some way, not separately. They will have a voice,” he said.

The U.S. and Zelensky want Europe to appoint a single person to negotiate with Moscow.

Russia, meanwhile, doesn’t want European countries involved in the direct negotiations, complaining they are financing and supplying Ukraine’s military effort. The Europeans are concerned about Russia’s conduct and broader intentions on the continent.

But Washington and European capitals have sometimes seemed at odds in their diplomatic efforts. 

Trump has repeatedly sided with Putin, last month waiving sanctions and striking a deal to import Russian diesel, in moves that dismayed Ukraine and European leaders.

The Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov argued that for Europe to join peace talks, it first must name a representative.

“The Europeans squabble like spiders in a jar. If someone takes the initiative to establish contact with the Russian side, such people are facing ostracism.”

Many in Europe also see the inclusion of Moscow in discussions about postwar European security as an unwelcome concession to Putin, who has described NATO’s eastward expansion as a main security threat and has demanded the alliance’s troops be pulled back from Russia’s borders.

Some analysts say negotiators may be looking to grant Russia concessions on NATO's strategy in return for peace in Ukraine – a possibility that alarms European leaders.

Thursday’s talks were “substantive, constructive, frank and useful,” Putin’s aide Yuri Ushakov said.

He added that the Kremlin leader reminded Witkoff and Kushner about Moscow’s proposals from 2021 – before it sent troops into Ukraine – demanding that NATO roll back the alliance’s military deployments in Central and Eastern Europe. 

Russia will update those with “fresh considerations,” Ushakov said.

Putin reaffirmed to the U.S. envoys that any European troops sent to Ukraine after a ceasefire — an idea long floated by Europe to prevent a new attack by Moscow — would be “absolutely unacceptable” and Russia would regard the deployment as a security threat and legitimate target. 

“In other words, the war would resume immediately,” the Russian president said.He also said Russia regards its border with Ukraine to be sealed by a prospective peace deal as now extending to cover the four Ukrainian regions that Moscow annexed in 2022 but never fully controlled.

Zelensky is in Dublin for a meeting of more than 40 European countries that also includes NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.

Rutte said the U.S., Europe and Ukraine are “very much aligned” on what security guarantees should look like, following a meeting in Paris in January. 

“But now of course we need the peace deal, or at least a ceasefire,” Rutte said.

Amid the negotiations, fighting continues along the 1,200-kilometer (about 750-mile) front line.

Russia’s bigger army has been held back by dogged Ukrainian resistance while Moscow’s drone and missile strikes on Ukraine’s energy facilities disrupted heat, electricity and water supplies to Ukrainian cities, sapping public morale in what Kyiv calls a “weaponization of winter.”

Russia’s Defense Ministry said its air defenses downed 71 Ukrainian drones overnight. Its forces struck a drone-manufacturing plant in Kyiv and three other facilities producing missile fuel and drone components in the area around the Ukrainian capital, the ministry said.Russia launched missiles and 123 drones, 73 of them jet-powered drones, at Ukraine overnight, the Ukrainian air force said. Hits were recorded at 17 locations, it said.

Ukraine is experiencing another slowdown in the U.S. Starshield system — SpaceX’s military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service — that the country needs to defend itself against Russian attacks, Zelensky said Thursday on social media.

Military units have recorded “significant disruptions,” including speed restrictions limiting Ukrainian drones to 161 kph (100 mph), Zelensky said, adding that a military investigation established that the restrictions weren't random errors.

Ukraine uses Starlink and Starshield for intercepting Russian drones and launching its own strikes.

Last month, limits on Ukrainian drone speeds severely disrupted operations and alarmed Kyiv officials who fear U.S. support could drop off.Elon Musk acknowledged that his company SpaceX had throttled the Starlink internet service in Ukraine for about a week, saying the system couldn’t be used for offensive strikes against Russia.

Zelensky said the speed limits cover operations in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine and that Kyiv is trying to find out from U.S. officials what is going on.

A Russian serviceman was killed in St. Petersburg early Thursday when his vehicle exploded, according to the Investigative Committee, the country’s main criminal investigation agency. 

It didn’t identify the victim or say who was behind the bombing. The Fontanka news outlet said the victim was a colonel and that a bomb in his car exploded as he drove off.

Several senior Russian military officers have died in bombings and other attacks that Moscow blames on Ukraine. Kyiv has claimed responsibility for some attacks on Russian soil.
news.summary: Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who is also President Donald Trump's son-in-law, brokered talks this week between delegations from Moscow and Kyiv

news.title: Democrats React to Nvidia Shock as They Prepare for Power: ‘Wake-Up Call’
news.text: The abrupt resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Thursday comes as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress following sweeping victories in the midterm elections last week. Judging by their reactions to his exit, which followed revelations of multiple affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese intelligence operative, Democrats intend to pursue answers well beyond his departure from the company. The national security implications loom large, given Nvidia's central role in the global artificial intelligence industry and Huang's close relationship with President Donald Trump, whose administration has eased some restrictions on the company's sales of advanced chips to China. Representative Joe Morelle, a New York Democrat, called Huang's resignation a "wake-up call.” "Well, it sounds like [Huang] admitted to more than one inappropriate relationship, so I think he did what was appropriate given the circumstances," Morelle told Newsweek on Thursday. "It's really a wake-up call in what is a critical position he has, and obviously in terms of national security and economic security.” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, meanwhile, made clear that Huang's resignation would not end congressional scrutiny of the matter. "Despite Jensen Huang's resignation, Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk," the New York Democrat wrote on X Thursday. Schumer also demanded answers from the Trump administration about what it knew of Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset and how it responded. "Were government officials told not to investigate because of Trump's relationship with Mr. Huang? What did Trump know when he personally invited Mr. Huang aboard Air Force One?" Schumer asked. "Americans deserve to know that those at the highest levels of power are putting America first, not their bottom line or their personal friendships." Newsweek reached out to Nvidia and the White House on Thursday for comment. Why It Matters Huang's departure after 33 years leading Nvidia has shaken one of the world's most consequential technology companies, whose chips are essential to the development of advanced AI systems. But the controversy extends beyond corporate leadership. The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence officials had identified Alice Huang, a Chinese business executive with whom Huang developed a relationship, as a potential intelligence operative for Beijing, raising questions about whether foreign intelligence services sought to influence a powerful executive involved in shaping U.S. technology policy. With Democrats preparing to assume control of Congress, the scandal could also intensify scrutiny of the Trump administration's handling of intelligence warnings and its relationship with Jensen Huang. What to Know Nvidia announced Thursday that Huang had resigned as president, CEO and a member of its board, effective immediately. The company appointed longtime Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO and said its board had begun searching for a permanent successor. Jensen Huang's exit followed reports that he had engaged in an extramarital affair with Alice Huang (no relation), whom U.S. intelligence reportedly identified as having been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security. According to the Times, the alleged intelligence operation sought information about American AI technology and potentially aimed to influence Nvidia to advocate for greater Chinese access to advanced U.S. chips. In an internal message sent to Nvidia staff, Jensen Huang acknowledged Sunday that he had been unfaithful to his wife. The Times subsequently reported Wednesday that he had also engaged in an affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare and one of his direct reports. Reuters, citing two people ‌familiar with the matter, on Thursday reported that the CEO also had a third affair, this time with another Nvidia employee. Newsweek has not independently confirmed the reporting. China has rejected the espionage allegations. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Monday that "the so-called Chinese spy allegation is unsubstantiated" and "nothing but smears against China." Nvidia's board said Sunday it had opened an independent investigation into the matter, adding it had "no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised." There has been no public evidence establishing that Huang knowingly acted on behalf of Chinese interests, knew of Alice Huang's alleged intelligence connections or altered his positions on U.S. export policy because of her. Trump said Monday that Huang had told him he "absolutely had no idea that the person in question was a spy,” adding that he believed him. Democrats Demand Answers Senator Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, said Thursday that Huang's resignation did not eliminate the need for accountability. "Jensen Huang's decision to resign from NVIDIA does not absolve him, other executives, or the company as a whole of responsibility for putting our national security at risk or for any potential violations of our laws," Warren wrote on X. Senator Mark Warner of Virginia, a senior Democrat on the Senate Intelligence Committee, raised broader concerns about the influence of technology executives on American national security policy. "I think it also raises a question, where we have these companies that are so powerful, whether it's Jensen Huang or Elon Musk, that they literally are driving national security policy," Warner told Newsweek. news.title: Chris Van Hollen Says He’s the ‘Underdog’ in Senate Majority Leader Challenge – But Has 10-Plus Pledges Against Schumer
news.text:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) formally launched his bid to challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) for Senate majority leader, while acknowledging that he’s the “underdog” in the race.

The senator from Maryland stopped by MS NOW’s “The Briefing with Jen Psaki” on Thursday, where he confirmed that he had decided to run for the Senate majority leader position.

“This is not about any one individual, but it is about answering the call of the American people,” he told host Jen Psaki. “We saw a huge outburst of democracy on Election Day — red states, blue states, purple states — and it wasn’t only a rejection of Donald Trump and his corruption and his wars and his cruelty, it was also about a call for a larger change to take on a broken economic system that’s rigged in favor of the very wealthy against working people, led by a corrupt political system.”

Per Van Hollen, the midterms results were a message from the public to “reject the status quo and to reject business as usual.” He added: “And to do that, I think we need new leadership.”

And so, Van Hollen is set to go against Schumer, who has been a leader on Capitol Hill for Democrats for nearly 10 years, during the election in December.

As for where Van Hollen stands in this fight? He called himself the “underdog.”

“Am I the underdog? Yes,” he said. “You’re talking about an incumbent who uses the power of incumbency to, you know, provide deals to people.”

However, Van Hollen defended that was “part of the problem,” adding, “We should have a little bit of democracy in the Senate Democratic Caucus. You mentioned some of the new people, you know, one of the things they heard on the campaign trail led them to say they’re not going to support our current majority leader.”

When grilled by Psaki on the number of pledges of support he’s received in private, Van Hollen said it was “more than 10,” adding, “We have a lot of people.”

Van Hollen’s announcement comes on the heels of Sens. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) declaring that they would not support Schumer as leader. Additionally, Senators-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) and Peggy Flanagan (D-Minn.) also voiced support for a Van Hollen bid this week.

news.title: Jensen Huang could testify before Congress after resigning as Nvidia CEO
news.text:
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is expected to testify before the US Congress within two weeks following his resignation on Thursday amid allegations involving a suspected Chinese spy.

According to The Guardian, House Foreign Affairs Committee chairman Brian Mast said congressional staff had contacted Nvidia to arrange Huang's testimony.

Huang stepped down following growing scrutiny of his relationship with Alice Huang, a woman suspected of working for Chinese intelligence. He has denied knowing about her alleged intelligence connections.

Reports of additional relationships involving Nvidia employees also increased pressure on the executive before the company's board discussed his future.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer has demanded answers about whether American national security was compromised.

He also questioned what President Donald Trump knew about the allegations before inviting Huang aboard Air Force One during a visit to Beijing.

“Americans deserve to know that those at the highest levels of power are putting America first, not their bottom line or their personal friendships,” Schumer said.

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries also called for a classified congressional briefing.

Jeffries described Huang's resignation as the “right thing” to do.

news.title: From fairy invasions to political intrigue, 10 new books worth your time
news.text:
Betrayal by Luke Harding (Faber, $37)A preparatory part of Vladimir Putin’s imperialist grab to colonise Ukraine in 2022 involved Russian special forces storming the presidential building in Kyiv, and either capturing or executing Volodymyr Zelensky and other heads of government. Like the rest of the war, it didn’t go to plan. Putin’s invasion is one part of Luke Harding’s examination of the betrayal of the rules-based international system – encoded in the 1945 UN Charter that instructed all members to “refrain” from “threat or force” for territorial gains – that has brought the world relative peace since the end of World War II.

The Ukraine war is a pivotal case study in charting this alarming trend (and the book includes a face-to-face with Zelensky). It also incorporates Donald Trump’s war in Iran, his Greenland threats, China and Taiwan and North Korea. Karl Marx wrote that history does repeat itself, the second time around as farce. Today’s unstable world bears eerie similarities to the 1930s, with a right collection of thugs, war criminals, dictators and would-be dictators rearing their ugly heads once again. History will reveal if it results in farce, or a category that Marx didn’t mention – tragic farce. A compelling piece of superior analytic journalism, timely, urgent and just a bit scary.

Australian Girls by Catherine Gay (Monash University Publishing, $40)As often as not, the term “girl” can be a put-down, but this study of 19th-century girls reclaims the word to empower them. It tells the stories of settler and Aboriginal girls (mostly between the ages of five and 15) from the 1840s to Federation – united, where possible, by surviving artefacts the girls made themselves, such as a handmade Commonwealth dress, school exercise books and diaries.

Academic Catherine Gay maintains that most histories write girls out of the narrative, asserting that she “takes girls seriously” and that her subjects “participated in and contributed to their families and society … and were key actors who contributed to historical change”. Whether she is documenting the activism of, say, Ellen, an Indigenous girl in the 1860s, or the impact of free education in the 1870s, the stories are told firmly from the girls’ point of view. While it may have started life as an academic study, Gay brings a welcome lightness of touch to a previously neglected history.

Jacques Miller by Caitlin McInnis (The Miegunyah Press, $50)This is not just a portrait of a great scientific mind, but of the relentless drive behind a game-changing discovery. The scientist is Australian Jacques Miller and, to a large extent, this is the story of his groundbreaking work on the thymus – an organ vital to the immune system – which transformed the study of immunology worldwide. Many argue that he ought to have received the Nobel Prize, and the fact that he was overlooked remains a sore point.
news.summary: From Susanna Clarke’s mischievous fairies to Kaz Cooke’s spooky ladies, our critics review new fiction and non-fiction.

news.title: Trump bluntly tells JD Vance to shift focus from Iran to targeting 'corruption and crime' at home
news.text: WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump on Thursday directed Vice President JD Vance to shift his focus away from the Iran war and instead devote himself to fighting what the president says is corruption and crime in Democratic-controlled cities and states.Vance, who served as the lead negotiator for a short-lived truce in the eight-month old war, has been blunt in blaming the war — and the economic reverberations it has caused — for Republicans' sweeping losses in last week's midterm elections in the United States.But Trump brusquely told the vice president in a social media post Thursday to shift his energies away from the Iran war to what he argues is a more pressing — and perhaps more politically salient — issue after Republicans were trounced at the polls.“We don’t need a deal with Iran,” Trump said in the post. “Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”Trump earlier this week said he believed the war “militarily is effectively over,” and appeared to double down on that message by pointedly directing Vance “to focus his complete and total attention” on his anti-fraud campaign.Democrats have promised intense oversight of Trump's business dealings and other targets when they take control of Congress in January after voters identified corruption as one of their top concerns. Trump's post about Vance and the Iran war was, in part, responding to a flurry of reports about Democrats' plans.But it also came after The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday evening that Vance was weighing engaging in a new round of direct talks with a senior Iranian official.The vice president's office did not respond to a request for comment.The White House press office, in an email, responded to a query by highlighting that Trump made clear in his post that he sees no need to negotiate with Iran..President Trump says US does not 'need a deal with Iran'.Vance blamed Trump's Iran war for midterm lossesVance, who had long advocated for restraint in U.S. military interventions overseas, was lukewarm in his defense of the conflict after Trump launched it and became the face of an unsuccessful attempt to end the fighting when he headed up negotiations over the summer.Following the Nov. 3 losses, Vance wrote a lengthy post on X in which he didn't mince words about the political impact of the conflict.“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so," Vance said. “Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest.”The vice president is considering whether to launch a 2028 run for the White House. Voter dissatisfaction with Trump's handling of the war could weigh down those ambitions.The president has yet to endorse a successor for the 2028 race. In a CBS “60 Minutes” interview that aired Sunday, the president said he “may or may not get involved” in offering an endorsement.Trump earlier this week said that he believed that mediation efforts led by Qatar are making progress and that it was unlikely he would need to make good on earlier threats to restart the full-scale bombardment of Iran after he was past the midterm elections.The president said in an interview on “The Hugh Hewitt Show” on Thursday that he stood ready to restart strikes if necessary. “If something doesn’t work out, I would not hesitate,” he said..Attacks in Strait of Hormuz reach highest level since start of war: security data.Separately, in an interview with commentator Stephen A. Smith, Trump suggested he hasn't ruled out carrying out strikes on Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, a facility linked to Iran's nuclear program, if the U.S. detects signs of activity at the facility.Waters around Iran remain treacherousOil shipments coming out of the Strait of Hormuz have recovered to near prewar levels after Iran effectively choked the critical waterway for months, stemming the flow of crude and energy resources from its Persian Gulf neighbors.But international tankers now are relying on U.S. Navy escorts to get the oil out of the strait. The U.S. military has recently carried out limited strikes on Iran, including against its air defenses.And while crude and liquefied natural gas exports from the Gulf are climbing, there's also been an uptick in attacks on ships trying to traverse the waterway.The British military on Thursday reported at least two tankers were struck by projectiles in recent days while traversing contested waters near Iran.The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Center, an agency that monitors maritime safety, said one of the tankers was struck Wednesday in the Strait of Hormuz, northwest of Ras al-Khaimah. The agency reported the crew evacuated safely and no casualties were reported.In another incident from Tuesday, the UKMTO said a tanker was struck by .Iran president accuses US, Israel of causing environmental damage during war.a projectile in the Persian Gulf. Multiple people were taken ashore for medical assistance while the remaining crew was safe and accounted for, the agency said. At the same time, a Saudi-led coalition is mired in fighting with Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen. That fighting has made it precarious to transport oil and other goods through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean.Qalibaf claims the U.S. wants Russia to interveneMeanwhile, Iran’s chief negotiator and parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, said in an interview that the United States has asked for Russian President Vladimir Putin to facilitate direct negotiations between the U.S. and Iran.“It was the Americans who, during a visit to Moscow, spoke with Mr. Putin and asked him to speak with Iran so that, in any case, Iran would agree to speak directly with them,” Qalibaf told Al Jazeera in the interview. “Look, Russia and Mr. Putin, the Russian president, are friends of ours. We have strategic relations with Russia. We are very close, and we hold Mr. Putin in particularly high regard."The White House did not directly respond to a query about whether the U.S. has asked Putin to facilitate talks with Iran.Qalibaf said the secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, Maj. Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, traveled to Russia and briefed Putin on details of the negotiations. “He informed him that we had conveyed our positions, which represent the legitimate rights and rightful demands of our people, to the Americans,” he said, adding that it is up to the U.S. side to respond.“It is up to them to decide. If they are truly telling the truth and are sincere about negotiations, then they should respond and begin the process,” Qalibaf said. “But if they want to pursue the path of war, then naturally, we are fully prepared for that as well.”.Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

news.title: Timeline of the stunning fall of powerful Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang
news.text:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's stunning resignation from the tech company he co-founded in 1993 comes amid investigations by federal authorities and his own board of directors into allegations that he had multiple extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

Huang, 63, had become a trusted ally of President Donald Trump and an adviser to the president on AI technology, visiting the White House for events more than a half-dozen times between January 2025 and October 2026. This year, he has traveled with Trump on a state visit to China and joined the president during a state visit to Great Britain.

A timeline pieced together by ABC News indicates that Huang and Chinese businesswoman and alleged spy Alice Huang (no relation) have known each other since at least 2024, and that Trump had been briefed twice over the past year on the relationship by intelligence officials and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

June 7, 2024 -- The first known photo of Jensen Huang and Alice Huang emerges of them sitting next to each other at Computex Taipei, the world's largest AI exhibition.

Jan. 31, 2025 -- President Donald Trump meets Jensen Huang for the first time during a meeting at the White House.

May 22, 2025 -- Jensen Huang and Alice Huang are captured on video by Taiwanese news outlet TVBS leaving a restaurant together in Taipei.

Fall of 2025 -- Trump is briefed on U.S. intelligence that Jensen Huang is having an affair with a woman believed to be working for Chinese intelligence, a U.S. official and sources briefed on the matter told ABC News. The president does not take any action at the time, the official and sources said.

Dec. 8, 2025 – Trump publicly announces a major policy change that would allow Nvidia to sell H200 AI chips to China in exchange for the U.S. receiving a 25% cut on the sales.

March 25, 2026 -- Trump appoints Jensen Huang as one of 13 members of the newly established President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.

April 28, 2026 -- Jensen Huang and his wife of more than 40 years, Lori, are guests at the state visit and state dinner honoring Britain's King Charles.

Spring 2026 -- A classified memo is drafted that warns top administration officials that Jensen Huang has a close relationship with a woman that U.S. intelligence officials believe to be a Chinese spy, sources familiar with the matter told ABC News, confirming reporting in The New York Times. 

May 12, 2026 -- Secretary of State Marco Rubio shares intelligence with President Trump on Air Force One showing Jensen Huang is in a relationship with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy, a U.S. official and two sources familiar with the matter have told ABC News. This is the second known time that Trump had been warned about the suspected espionage plot, sources with knowledge of the situation tell ABC News.

Trump's briefing from Rubio, first reported in The New York Times, came shortly before Huang joined the president on a state visit to China, according to the U.S. official and sources. Huang was initially not listed among the CEOs joining Trump's China trip, but he joined the president's entourage in Alaska after news reports noted his absence. Trump later posted on his Truth Social platform that Huang was on Air Force One with him.

Sept. 24, 2026 -- Jensen Huang and his wife, Lori, attend a state dinner at the White House hosted by Trump during Chinese Leader Xi Jinping's state visit to the United States.

Oct. 8, 2026 -- Huang attends the "Golden Age of American Innovation" summit at U.S. Institute of Peace in Washington, D.C., where Trump honors him with a National Medal for Science and Technology and Innovation.

Oct. 29, 2026 -- The New York Times reports that Huang and Alice Huang, an executive at the Singaporean tech company Megaspeed, had a "close relationship."

Oct. 31, 2026 -- The Wall Street Journal reports that intelligence officials in the U.S., Singapore and Taiwan had reason to believe that Alice Huang might be a Chinese spy.

Nov. 8, 2026 -- Jensen Huang releases a memo to colleagues acknowledging "I was unfaithful to my wife." He goes on to say, "I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it." He also apologizes to his colleagues, the Nvidia board, partners and shareholders, saying, "My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility."

Nvidia's board of directors announces it is launching an independent investigation into allegations that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort." The board says that while it "has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information."

Nov. 9, 2026 -- Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun tells reporters, "The claim regarding a so-called Chinese spy is completely groundless and pure slander."

That same day, President Trump tells reporters he has spoken to Jensen Huang on the phone. "He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy," Trump says at a press briefing.

Nov. 10, 2026 -- The Republican chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Rep. Brian Mast, tells ABC News he's prepared to subpoena Jensen Huang if he does not respond to a request from several House Republicans for a closed-door briefing on Huang's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.

Nov. 11, 2026 -- The New York Times reports that Huang allegedly had a second extramarital relationship with an Nvidia executive who reports to him. The Wall Street Journal reports that Nvidia's Board of Directors is reportedly planning to oust Jensen Huang as the company's CEO.

Nov. 12, 2026 -- Nvidia announces Jensen Huang has resigned as the company's CEO and that Colette Kress, executive vice president and CFO of Nvidia, has been appointed the company's interim CEO as the board initiates a search for a permanent replacement for Huang.
news.summary: While the depths of the scandal have yet to be disclosed, here is a timeline of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

news.title: Oil prices set for second weekly decline as Trump to stay with Iran blockade
news.text:
PERTH: Oil prices were mixed on Friday, but set for their second weekly decline, as the US plans to continue its Iranian blockade, reducing the chance of renewed large-scale fighting ​that could disrupt Middle East supplies, though attacks on shipping remain a danger.

Brent futures were ‌little changed, down 1 cent at $95.41 a barrel at 0242 GMT. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) declined by 20 cents, or 0.25%, to $88.52 a barrel.

Friday’s declines reversed two days of gains amid a volatile trading week with earlier hopes for a rapprochement ​of the US-Israel war against Iran, now in its ninth month, offset by strikes on Saudi ​Arabian infrastructure by Yemen’s Houthis and attacks on tankers transporting crude out ⁠of the Gulf.

Despite the swings in prices amid the inconclusive war, Brent is set for a 2.4% ​drop this week, after plunging 16% the previous week, while WTI is set for a 2.5% decline, ​after dropping 13% previously.

Prices slipped on Friday after US President Donald Trump said on Truth Social a deal with Iran was not necessary to end the war, indicating he will stick with the blockade on oil shipments and trade and economic ​sanctions.

The overall decline in prices over the past two weeks reflects a good assessment of the risks ​to the market, said Chris Brankin, global advisor for Melbourne-based brokerage MiTrade.

“I think the oil market is priced to perfection ‌at ⁠this point,” he said, adding that prices have bounced back a bit but without much conviction on the part of traders, which shows they are following closely what is happening in the Middle East.

Despite the easing prices, risks remain for oil shipments out of the Strait of Hormuz, the key waterway for crude ​exports from the main ​Middle East producers.

On Thursday, ⁠Iran’s military said four oil tankers were hit by explosions in the Strait of Hormuz after ignoring warnings. Reuters could not immediately verify the Iranian accounts.

That ​same day, Yemen’s Houthis said they had attacked a pumping station on the ​Saudi East-West ⁠oil pipeline; an oil facility in the Saudi Red Sea city of Yanbu; and an Aramco building in the capital Riyadh.

Also pressuring prices, US crude and fuel inventories rose last week, driven by softer refined products demand ⁠and ​a jump in oil imports, the Energy Information Administration said on ​Thursday.

Crude inventories rose by 4.7 million barrels to 414.4 million barrels in the week ended November 6, the EIA said, compared with ​analysts’ expectations in a Reuters poll for a 1.1 million-barrel draw.

news.text:

Michael Wolff is a longtime author and reporter best known for his extensive coverage of Trump's political career, including several books about his first term and another about his return to office. And now Wolff says he’s seeing history repeat itself in the second Trump administration — with similarly pathetic consequences for Trump.

The Trump administration is attempting to push back against incoming Democratic leaders with a letter from the president's top lawyer "taking an aggressive — and hugely controversial — stance" against the party's new oversight plans. 

But good luck defending a homefront with no army, said Wolff in a Thursday night “Inside Trump’s Head” podcast.

“[After January 3rd] … we are going to see Trump and the Trump Administration go to war with the Democrats and with Congress, but there's going to be problems with that,” said Wolff. “Nobody [competent] works for the Justice Department anymore.” 

“So many people have been leaving,” said show co-host Joanna Cole. 

“Right. Most of the people he has had on his side to wage war are leaving. It is going to be Donald Trump and [Chief of Staff] Steven Miller. That is it.”

Normally, Trump could also count his defense attorney from his hush-money conviction as being in his corner — since Trump brought him on as Attorney General. But Wolff said Blanche “is in deep, and he's got to start protecting himself” from legal liability.
