news.title: Jensen Huang Reportedly Had Third Affair; Nvidia Exit Caps Week of Scandal
news.text: Jensen Huang had an intimate relationship with a second Nvidia employee, Reuters reported Thursday, citing two people familiar with the matter. It is the third extramarital relationship attributed to the 63-year-old, and it emerged only after Nvidia’s board had accepted his resignation from the company he had led for 33 years. Reuters did not name the woman or describe her role at Nvidia, and said its attempts to reach her were unsuccessful. Nvidia declined to comment. Jensen Huang and a representative for the company's board did not respond to the news agency's requests. Newsweek has reached out to Nvidia for comment. The disclosure lands on a figure who, until days ago, seemed less a chief executive than the artificial intelligence economy’s indispensable man. On Thursday morning, Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang had resigned as president, CEO and director, effective immediately. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO while keeping her finance role, and longtime director Harvey C. Jones becomes the board's first-ever chair. The board said it would consider internal and external candidates for the permanent post. A Week of Unraveling From confession to exit, the collapse took less than a week. On Sunday, Jensen Huang sent employees a letter confessing he had been unfaithful to his wife. "Leading Nvidia is the privilege of my life," he wrote. "I have fallen short of that responsibility." He did not say with whom. The New York Times had already reported that U.S. intelligence officials suspected Alice Huang—a Chinese citizen, former television reporter and onetime executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, one of Nvidia's largest customers in Southeast Asia—was gathering information for Beijing and had grown close to him. The two are not related. That same day, Nvidia's board opened an independent investigation into reports that Jensen Huang had been "the target of a foreign intelligence effort," and declared its "confidence in Jensen and his leadership team." Company spokesperson John Rizzo was blunter: "Today's news will not slow Nvidia." The confidence lasted days. On Wednesday, The Wall Street Journal reported that directors were preparing to push Jensen Huang out over two affairs. The second, the Times reported, citing five people who had worked at Nvidia, involved Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, who reported directly to him. Two sources told the paper the pair had been filmed being affectionate at a San Jose, California, hotel during the company's developer conference in March; three people briefed on the episode said Jensen Huang's security detail isolated the bystander who recorded it and offered a nondisclosure agreement. The Times said it had not seen the footage. When the paper called, Jensen Huang said, "I don't think you should be talking to me directly," and hung up. Powell did not respond to the Times. Both are married to other people. The board accepted his resignation that night, according to a regulatory filing, and Nvidia announced it Thursday morning. The announcement did not address either relationship. It thanked Jensen Huang for his "immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry." Kress said she was "committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years." The Market Blinks Nvidia shares plunged 14 percent at the opening bell as investors confronted a widening thicket of lawsuits and investigations, and a market that leans heavily on a handful of tech giants. The stock quickly recovered half that loss and closed down 4.3 percent, extending a slide that had already erased 27 percent of its value from an October record through Wednesday. Nvidia reports quarterly earnings Tuesday—its first without its founder at the helm. The company also faces a shareholder class action alleging that it and Jensen Huang inflated the share price by failing to disclose the affair. The founding story is Silicon Valley scripture: In 1993, Jensen Huang and two fellow engineers met at a Denny's in San Jose with an idea for a faster video-game graphics chip. What grew from that meeting became the engine of the AI boom, a multitrillion-dollar company jostling with Apple and Microsoft atop the S&P 500. Jensen Huang, whose fortune Forbes estimates at more than $150 billion, remains its largest individual shareholder. He had also pressed Washington to loosen limits on chip sales to China. The Question Beneath the Scandal That lobbying is how a story about infidelity became a matter of national security. Megaspeed became Nvidia's largest Southeast Asian customer, buying $4.6 billion in advanced processors from 2023 to 2025, according to a September report by the research group C4ADS, which described an alleged operation to route the chips to blacklisted Chinese end users. Megaspeed has denied the allegations. Singapore authorities seized Alice Huang's passport after questioning her last year. They stopped short of finding a crime, but suspected she had given "inaccurate information" about her role, and barred her from returning. Taiwan's interior minister told lawmakers her right to enter had been revoked indefinitely. Beijing has called the spy allegation "nothing but smears against China." Much remains unproven. Newsweek could not independently verify several details of Alice Huang’s background. In a post titled “Espionage, AI and the Risks of Strategic Overreaction,” William Hannas and Huey Meei-Chang of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology argued that any response must be grounded in evidence. And on Sunday, before the second and third relationships were reported, Nvidia’s board said it had “no reason to believe” that national security or company secrets had been compromised. Even inside the U.S. government, the case against Alice Huang is not settled. Multiple sources told CNN on Thursday that the intelligence gathered so far does not prove she was spying for Beijing, and that officials disagree over how strong the evidence is that China’s Ministry of State Security recruited her. Yet the worry has not gone away. One person familiar with the investigation told the network that U.S. intelligence obtained communications suggesting someone with close access to Jensen Huang and Nvidia was the source of information that surfaced in Chinese intelligence channels. And a former Commerce Department official offered a sharper observation: Given Jensen Huang’s public push to sell more chips to China, “an intelligence operation wasn’t necessary to achieve that result.” Washington Is Not Finished President Donald Trump, who has hosted Jensen Huang at the White House and aboard Air Force One, said Monday that the executive told him he “had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.” On Thursday, Trump said Jensen Huang had “done a fantastic job.” Asked by Stephen A. Smith in an interview for Smith’s Straight Shooter whether Jensen Huang should have stepped down, Trump said: “Was the woman a spy? I don’t know if that has been determined yet, but if the woman was a spy, yes; if the woman was not a spy, perhaps it would be different.” Lawmakers were less forgiving. Representative John Moolenaar, the Michigan Republican who chairs the House Select Committee on China, pointedly called it a "firing" and "an unfortunate end that could have been avoided." Nvidia, he said, "must now change its corporate practices and appoint leadership that makes national security its top priority." Senator Elizabeth Warren, the Massachusetts Democrat, said the resignation "does not absolve" Jensen Huang, other executives or the company of responsibility "for putting our national security at risk." Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said Congress must still get answers from Jensen Huang and others at Nvidia. Representative Brian Mast, the Florida Republican who chairs the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said his panel had been in contact with Jensen Huang's team as recently as Wednesday night, and that a subpoena would follow if necessary. Senator Tim Scott, the South Carolina Republican who chairs the Senate Banking Committee, asked Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify, writing on X that “the American people deserve answers.” In a letter dated Thursday, Scott invited Jensen Huang to a December 3 public hearing and warned that the committee could use subpoenas if he did not appear voluntarily. Not everyone was keeping score. Hours before the resignation was announced, as reports of an ouster swirled, Elon Musk answered a post on X urging him to hire Jensen Huang: "That would be an honor." In his Sunday letter, Jensen Huang told employees his responsibility was "to serve you and be worthy of your trust." Within days, he was gone—and the trust he wrote of had become a matter for investigators, lawmakers and a board searching for the company's first permanent chief executive since that meeting at Denny's. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Samantha Beech and Edward T. Cummins
news.summary: Hours after Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO, Reuters reported that he had a relationship with a second employee.

news.title: Jensen Huang built the company that powers AI. Now Nvidia must find a way forward without him
news.text:
APJensen Huang has stepped down as Nvidia CEO following scandals involving alleged affairs and links to a suspected Chinese spy, leaving the AI chip giant facing leadership uncertainty and congressional scrutiny.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday, capping a spectacular downfall for a poster boy of the artificial intelligence boom whose exit following reports of extramarital affairs now thrusts the chipmaker into an uncertain future.After a dizzying series of headlines about Huang's infidelity and ties to an alleged Chinese spy, his departure sets off a scramble to find a permanent replacement to lead the multitrillion-dollar colossus that grew from obscurity to a perch between Apple and Microsoft at the top of the S&P index.Also read: The Huawei connection: Alleged Chinese spy in Jensen Huang affair linked to Nvidia rivalThe resignation sent shares of Nvidia plummeting 14% at the opening bell, before stabilizing. The stock closed down about 4% Thursday as investors pondered the lawsuits, investigations, likely corporate jockeying and the resilience of a market driven by the gains of a few tech giants."Huang's departure introduces uncertainty well beyond the company itself," said Asa Hiken, senior analyst for research firm eMarketer, reflecting fears of wider implications and the possibility of an AI bubble.Live EventsThe company named Colette Kress, the executive vice president and chief financial officer, as interim chief executive. She became CFO in 2013, overseeing the company's global finance operations. Before that, she worked for three years at Cisco and spent 13 years at Microsoft.Nvidia had no succession plan to prepare for the possibility of the departure of Huang, who was synonymous with Nvidia for more than 30 years in much the same way Steve Jobs embodied Apple. Nvidia said its board would consider internal and external candidates to replace him.In a statement Thursday, Kress said that Nvidia's "strength has always come from its people" and that she was "committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years."The board of directors said Thursday it had also named its first-ever chairman, Harvey C. Jones, an entrepreneur and venture investor.Drumbeat of scandals grew louderHuang, 63, is one of the world's wealthiest people, with a personal fortune that Forbes estimates at more than $150 billion. He is the single largest individual shareholder of Nvidia stock.A drumbeat of scandals around him had grown louder in recent weeks after The New York Times reported Huang's relationship with a woman the paper said U.S. officials had concluded was a Chinese spy who was recruited to influence California-based Nvidia to make its most advanced chips more available in China.The discovery set off alarms as high as the White House.U.S. President Donald Trump said Monday that the FBI was investigating but remained complimentary of Huang on Thursday, saying he "has done a fantastic job." Like many top tech CEOs, Huang is close to Trump, who has hosted him at the White House and on Air Force One, and awarded him a National Medal of Science.Nvidia's board announced an investigation into the allegations on Sunday, but said it remained confident in Huang's leadership. Then pressure compounded late Wednesday after reports surfaced of another alleged affair by Huang, this time with an Nvidia employee who reported to him. Reuters reported Thursday that Huang had an intimate relationship with a second employee, citing unidentified sources.The company has said it had "no reason to believe" that either national security or its secrets were compromised, but that its inquiry would examine all available information.Nvidia is due to report earnings Tuesday.Also read: US Senate panel seeks testimony from Jensen Huang, Commerce Secretary Lutnick over China spy concernsLawmakers still want to question HuangAfter Huang's exit, U.S. lawmakers were still insisting on questioning him about his interactions with a Chinese businesswoman named Alice Huang and the company's security protocols against espionage."Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk," Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer of New York posted online.Rep. Brian Mast, chairman of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, said the committee was in contact with Huang's team as recently as Wednesday night after putting in an initial request for an interview on Nov. 5. Mast said Huang would receive a subpoena to compel his appearance, if necessary.Alice Huang, the suspected spy at the center of the scandal, is a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International. Jensen Huang acknowledged an affair but did not identify her.The two are not related.Megaspeed faced allegations last year that it was illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China, but in December said there was "no evidence" of such exports.Singaporean authorities said Thursday that they questioned Alice Huang and confiscated her passport last year as part of an investigation into Megaspeed. They concluded that there wasn't enough evidence that she had committed a crime but suspected she provided "inaccurate information" to downplay her role at Megaspeed and barred her from returning to the country.China denies attempting to ensnare executiveChina has denied that it attempted to ensnare Jensen Huang. Nvidia has become a leader in making chips that power AI, and Huang has lobbied Washington to loosen limits on sales of Nvidia chips to China. In January, he won Trump's approval to sell Nvidia's H200 chips to China.Megaspeed said Thursday that it has cooperated with the U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, which handles enforcement of national security restrictions on technology exports, and was ready to "cooperate fully with any other relevant U.S. government authority."The company said it has hired a U.S. law firm to conduct a "comprehensive census" of its computer chips and to verify its export controls."Megaspeed welcomes appropriate government scrutiny and is committed to demonstrating through concrete actions that it operates responsibly, transparently, and in accordance with applicable U.S. laws," it said.Apart from questions over national security, Megaspeed's finances also have drawn attention. Its total assets soared roughly 90-fold from late 2023 to 2024, to almost $3 billion, according to Singapore corporate records.Revenue surged to over $294 million in 2024 from none in 2023.What comes next for Jensen Huang is unclear, though another tech mogul, Elon Musk, said on X that it "would be an honor" to hire him.At a time of growing alarm about AI's potential risks, Huang has been a voice of optimism on the technology's potential. His climb to the top of the corporate world started with an idea born in an unglamorous setting.Huang and two other engineers gathered in 1993 at a Denny's in San Jose, California, where they discussed building a computer chip that would make graphics for video games faster and more realistic.That conversation led to the founding of Nvidia.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: Jorge Taiana: 'It will be difficult for Cristina Fernández de Kirchner to stand as a candidate in 2027'
news.text:
In an interview with Modo Fontevecchia, broadcast on the +Perfil television channel and Radio Perfil (AM 1190), former foreign minister Jorge Taiana explained the status of ex-president Cristina Fernández de Kirchner’s submission to the United Nations challenging her lifetime ban from holding public office, though he acknowledges that the judicial timetable could make it difficult for her to stand in the 2027 election.

Taiana is a sociologist and political figure who currently serves as a national deputy for Buenos Aires Province. During his career, he has held several senior top government positions, including serving as defence minister from 2021 to 2023 under then-president Alberto Fernández, and as a national senator for Buenos Aires Province from 2019 to 2021.

He also served as foreign minister from 2005 to 2010, under the administrations of Néstor Kirchner and Cristina Fernández de Kirchner. In addition, he was executive secretary of the Organisation of American States' Inter-American Commission on Human Rights (IACHR) from 1996 to 2001 and Argentina's ambassador to Guatemala from 1992 to 1996.

Good morning, Jorge. It’s a pleasure to speak to you. We’re here in Buenos Aires and you’re over there; I’m told you’ve already left Washington and are now in New York. 

You took part, alongside national deputy Vanesa Siley, in a programme of meetings in Washington with organisations such as the Washington Office on Latin America (WOLA). 

Tell us a little about what you saw there, and how you view US relations with Argentina following [Donald] Trump's defeat, while you were there in Washington.

Well, I would say this is almost a post-shock moment, because the Democrats' electoral victory [in the US midterms] was bigger than expected. Not only do they have majorities in both chambers, but there have also been Republican defeats that are very difficult to understand. For example, Vice-President JD Vance, who is one of the possible contenders to succeed Trump, lost in his district and also lost with his Senate candidate; he has been dealt a blow.

Likewise, in Kansas, a Democratic senator was elected for the first time since 1930. And, obviously, the Republicans' defeat in Texas, where they had governed since the Reagan era, more than 40 years ago, has been a major shock.

In other words, this was essentially a rejection of Trump's policies: Trump is the big loser, and the Republican Party is suffering as a result. On the Democratic side, there have also been a series of changes: the emergence of a new generation of leaders, whose best-known faction is what is called the “democratic socialists.”

But, more broadly, there is a wider movement known as progressive Democrats – or sometimes populists – who have visions of change. There is a generational shift taking place within the party that has yet to run its course ...

Yesterday we had a very good meeting with two members of the Progressive Caucus: one was a very important congresswoman, Pramila Jayapal, who is of Indian origin and won more than 70 percent of the vote in her district in Washington state, on the Pacific coast; and the other was Jesús 'Chuy' García, a congressman from Chicago – which, as he pointed out to me, is the Pope's home city.

We spoke, of course, about Pope Leo XIV, who was in Argentina, where the huge scale of the public gatherings also made an impression.

Jorge, you mentioned US Vice-President JD Vance. Yesterday it was announced that he had cancelled his visit to Argentina, which had been scheduled for some time. How do you interpret this cancellation and what effect do you think Trump's defeat will have on relations with Argentina?

Well, it seems to me that the privileged relationship Milei secured – which led to them sending him the currency swap and buying pesos, in what was an unprecedented move – prompted a reaction from Democrats in Congress at the time, and that reaction has continued. In other words, from the standpoint of US economic policy abroad, and particularly towards Argentina, there is growing criticism and mistrust of the policies pursued by Bessent. So Argentina's position is not an easy one, and the idea that 'they'll give me money whenever I need it' and all the rest is now being cast into doubt by Trump's defeat ...

It seems to me that the narrative, as people call it nowadays, is running out for Milei's camp, and it is beginning to run into trouble. And Caputo is coming under increasing criticism, no longer just from the opposition, but also from prominent economists who had been very close to the government and had firmly supported it.

Jorge, you were also involved in an issue concerning former president Cristina Fernández de Kirchner and her petition to the United Nations, which was ultimately not considered and was postponed until the autumn in our hemisphere. I think this rules out any possibility of her being a candidate. 

I would like to hear your thoughts on the progress of the legal appeal before the United Nations, which seeks to restore the former president's political rights and allow her to stand as a candidate.

Well, there are two aspects to this. We have also come here to raise the broader issue of the deterioration of the situation, not only the authoritarianism of the Executive and how it manages, in a way, to secure support through favours in the Legislature, building a majority that is not ideological but based on financial support for particular or general purposes – there is clearly a majority in Congress that has been constructed quite artificially with money and is largely subordinate – but also the growing deterioration of the Judiciary.

Cristina is in prison and has been deprived of her political rights for life, while the President is deemed to have had nothing to do with [the] '$LIBRA' [cryptocurrency scandal], and the matter is then closed. And in the case of [former Cabinet chief Manuel] Adorni, they say it cannot be proved that he obtained that money while in office, when in fact we all know that in cases of illicit enrichment the burden of proof is reversed: it is the person under investigation who must demonstrate the legitimate origin of their money or assets. And that is obviously what has not happened in Adorni's case.

When you look at all of this, at Cristina's case and the issues that have arisen during the judicial proceedings, it becomes clear that there is political persecution of Cristina, and that has been evident at every level. If you look at the 'Vialidad' trial, it is a trial with a great many irregularities, both in terms of the National Constitution and the United Nations International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights.

That is why Cristina's legal team decided to submit a complaint to the Human Rights Committee, which has three components. One concerns her disqualification from holding public office, an issue that is of interest in the international human rights community. We held an important private meeting with legal experts from American University, we met with WOLA – a longstanding human rights organisation in Washington – and we will be meeting with organisations here in New York.

There is interest in examining the case because the Human Rights Committee has issued few rulings on situations involving this particular issue: when an additional penalty is greater than the principal sentence. In other words, Cristina was sentenced to six years in prison but also given a lifetime ban from holding public office. Lifetime disqualification exists under Argentine law, but the Committee has said many times that it should not exist – not specifically in Argentina, but in general. It opposes lifetime disqualification as a principle and recommends that it be abolished. That is one of the issues.

The second concerns all the violations of due process, and the third relates to the conditions of detention. The due-process violations concern several matters, above all the inability to present evidence: everything she submitted was rejected, and ultimately the Supreme Court did not consider the matter, applying Article 280 and effectively dismissing the appeal.

So the case goes to the Committee. What for? So that, through a favourable ruling – which is why precautionary measures were requested – the Committee can pave the way for a review of the sentence. That is what the Committee should recommend.

As for violations by the Argentine Judiciary of rights enshrined in the Covenant, it is clear that Cristina will win that case. The problem is that these proceedings at the United Nations, before the Committee – as would have been the case before the Inter-American Commission – take a long time: at least a couple of years.

So what matters most here is the request for precautionary measures to allow a review. Why? Because Article 366, subsection (f), of the Federal Code of Criminal Procedure allows a case to be reviewed following rulings by international bodies – for example, the Inter-American Court, the International Criminal Court, the International Court of Justice, or treaty bodies established under agreements signed by the country.

Indeed, a review under Article 366 can be requested even without an international ruling or a recommendation such as one from the Committee. It can, for example, be requested if there is new evidence, and Cristina's lawyers say there is new evidence in another case that forms part of the evidence Cristina was unable to present.

I was personally very doubtful that the Committee would issue a ruling so quickly. We have to remember that this was submitted at the end of July or in September, when the holidays begin in Europe and the northern hemisphere, and this is the Committee's first meeting since that break.

So they have received the case but have not ruled either on the precautionary measures or on the admissibility of the case. I think that was the most likely outcome. Some people were more optimistic and believed a decision might be made now. I did not think so. I believe they will study it further. Moreover, precautionary measures are generally granted in more limited circumstances, such as cases involving a threat to life, and so on ...

A decision by the United Nations Human Rights Committee would provide significant political and legal reinforcement for Cristina's claim that she did not receive a fair trial – a claim for which there are many grounds to challenge the proceedings.

More specifically, as you yourself said, you were not as optimistic as some others – whose optimism was contrary to reason – about the possibility of obtaining a ruling within a timeframe that would allow Cristina to stand as a candidate in the next elections. She will not be able to stand in the next elections.

Well, we'll have to see. A review can be requested through the domestic courts, and there could be a decision in March...

Let's say I'm not ruling it out. I think it will be difficult, but it is not something we can consider 100 percent settled.
